## Statement

Let $n\ge0$, let $p$ be a nonzero real polynomial of degree at most $n$, and
let $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ be real numbers. The values $p(x_i)$ cannot all be
nonzero with alternating signs.

1.1 By [F1], $p$ is continuous on each $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Since the endpoint values are nonzero and have opposite signs, [F2] gives a root $z_i\in(x_i,x_{i+1})$ for every $0\le i\le n$. These open intervals are pairwise disjoint, so the $z_i$ are $n+1$ distinct real roots. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The $n+1$ distinct roots from step 1.1 contradict [F3], because $p$ is nonzero and has degree at most $n$. Therefore the assumed alternating nonzero values cannot occur. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

1.1 Let $s(t)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\mathbf1_{E_j}(t)$ be a simple function with disjoint measurable $E_j$. Extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. By [F2], $\|\mathbf1_{E_j}(\cdot-h)-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_{L^p(\mathbb R)}\to0$ for each $j$; the triangle inequality and the finite sum show $\|s(\cdot-h)-s\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}\to0$. [F2, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $\rho_\delta$ be a nonnegative smooth scalar function supported in $[-\delta,\delta]$ with integral one. Apply the Bochner norm bound in [F4] pointwise to the convolution difference, then apply scalar integral Minkowski to $F(t,s)=\rho_\delta(s)\|f(t-s)-f(t)\|_X$. A Borel version of the strongly measurable $f$ may be used: replace the finitely many level sets in each simple approximant by Borel sets modulo null sets using [F3], then take its almost-everywhere limit. The resulting two-variable norm is measurable, and its section norms are at most $2\rho_\delta(s)\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}$, an integrable majorant. Thus [F4] gives on any compact subinterval $K\subset(0,T)$ $$\|\rho_\delta*f-f\|_{L^p(K;X)} \le\int\rho_\delta(s)\|f(\cdot-s)-f\|_{L^p(K;X)}\,ds.$$ The translation modulus from step 2.1 tends to zero uniformly for $|s|\le\delta$; hence the right-hand side tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the mollification claim. [F3, F4, step 2.1]

## Statement

are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

1.2 For an interval partition $\mathcal P$, let $P_\mathcal P f$ be the average of $f$ on each cell $I$. By [F4], $\|\,|I|^{-1}\int_I f\|_X\le |I|^{-1}\int_I\|f\|_X$. For $p>1$, scalar Hölder gives $|I|\|\,|I|^{-1}\int_I f\|_X^p\le\int_I\|f\|_X^p$; for $p=1$ the first inequality gives the same assertion directly. Summing proves contraction on $L^p$. To justify density for arbitrary completed Lebesgue level sets, write $E=B\cup N$ with $B$ Borel and $N$ contained in a Borel null set $Z$ by [F3], after intersecting all sets with $(0,T)$. The Borel set $B\cup Z$ differs from $E$ by a null set. Choose an open superset $O$ with excess less than $\eta$. The bounded open set $O\cap(0,T)$ is the union of the countably many rational-endpoint open intervals contained in it. Enumerate those intervals, and let $J_m$ be their first $m$ unions. By continuity from below [F3], $|(O\cap(0,T))\setminus J_m|\to0$. Thus a finite union of intervals differs from $E$ in measure by less than $2\eta$ for large $m$. Round the finitely many endpoints by continuous linear ramps, whose error is supported in intervals of arbitrarily small total length. It follows that continuous $X$-valued functions are dense in $L^p(0,T;X)$ by applying this construction to the finitely many level sets of a simple approximation [F1]. For continuous $g$, uniform continuity gives $\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}\le T^{1/p}\sup_{|s-t|\le\max|I|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|_X\to0$. Contraction now yields $\|P_\mathcal P f-f\|_{L^p}\le2\|f-g\|_{L^p}+\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}$, proving the averages assertion. [F1, F3, F4, A1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $\rho_\delta$ be a nonnegative smooth scalar function supported in $[-\delta,\delta]$ with integral one. Apply the Bochner norm bound in [F4] pointwise to the convolution difference, then apply scalar integral Minkowski to $F(t,s)=\rho_\delta(s)\|f(t-s)-f(t)\|_X$. A Borel version of the strongly measurable $f$ may be used: replace the finitely many level sets in each simple approximant by Borel sets modulo null sets using [F3], then take its almost-everywhere limit. The resulting two-variable norm is measurable, and its section norms are at most $2\rho_\delta(s)\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}$, an integrable majorant. Thus [F4] gives on any compact subinterval $K\subset(0,T)$ $$\|\rho_\delta*f-f\|_{L^p(K;X)} \le\int\rho_\delta(s)\|f(\cdot-s)-f\|_{L^p(K;X)}\,ds.$$ The translation modulus from step 2.1 tends to zero uniformly for $|s|\le\delta$; hence the right-hand side tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the mollification claim. [F3, F4, step 2.1]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D=(0,1)^2$, $b\in C^\infty(\overline D)$ vanish on $\partial D$, and choose $\rho\in C^\infty([0,\infty))$ equal to $1$ on $[0,1/3]$ and $0$ on $[1,\infty)$. Set $d_1=x$, $d_2=1-x$, $d_3=y$, $d_4=1-y$, and
$$R_\ell(x,y)=1-\prod_{i=1}^4(1-\rho(d_i/\ell)),\qquad 0<\ell<1/16.$$
This function is $1$ near the boundary and supported in strips of total area at most $4\ell$. There is $C$, independent of $\ell$, such that
$$\|\nabla(bR_\ell)\|_\infty\le C,\qquad \|D^k(bR_\ell)\|_2\le C\ell^{3/2-k}\quad(k=1,2,3).$$
For $\ell(t)=\sqrt t$, $0<t<T<1/256$,
$$\|\partial_t\nabla(bR_{\sqrt t})\|_2\le Ct^{-1}t^{1/4}.$$
If $m\in C^1((0,T))$, $\operatorname{rot}\psi=(\psi_y,-\psi_x)$, and $r=-m\operatorname{rot}(bR_{\sqrt t})$, then
$$\|r\|_\infty\le C|m|,\quad \|r\|_2\le C|m|t^{1/4},\quad \|\nabla r\|_2\le C|m|t^{-1/4},$$
$$\|r_t\|_2+\|\Delta r\|_2\le C(|m'|t^{1/4}+|m|t^{-3/4}).$$
Moreover $bR_\ell=0$ and $\partial_n(bR_\ell)=\partial_n b$ on each side. Thus if a smooth stream $\Psi$ has zero boundary value and $\partial_n\Psi=m\partial_n b$, then $\Psi-mbR_\ell$ has both zero value and zero normal derivative there, and its rotation has zero velocity trace. On any fixed $J\Subset(0,1)$ and sufficiently small $t$, the additional estimate $\|\partial_xr\|_{L^\infty(J\times(0,1))}\le C_J|m|$ holds.

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and satisfy
$a<x\cdot e<b$ for a unit vector $e$ and all $x\in\Omega$, with $a<b$.
Then every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le(b-a)\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The argument assumes Countable Choice through the stated Sobolev,
product-measure, and affine change-of-variables interfaces; it does not use the
Axiom of Choice.

1.1 First let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. Write $x=x_\perp+te$ with $x_\perp\perp e$. For fixed $x_\perp$ and $a<t<b$, the fundamental theorem [F1] gives $\varphi(x_\perp+te)=\int_a^t\partial_e\varphi(x_\perp+se)\,ds$, since the zero extension vanishes at $t=a$. Holder's inequality [F4], applied on $(a,t)$ and then enlarged to $(a,b)$, yields $|\varphi(x_\perp+te)|^2\le(b-a)\int_a^b|\partial_e\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^2\,ds$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Integrate step 1.1 over $t\in(a,b)$ and $x_\perp\in e^\perp$. Choose an orthonormal basis of $e^\perp$ and let $Q$ have those basis vectors followed by $e$ as its columns. Then $T(y)=Qy$ sends $(y_\perp,t)$ to $x_\perp+te$; Tonelli [F2] and $Q^TQ=I$, $|\det Q|=1$ in [F3] give the coordinate integral over the slab. The zero extension of $\varphi$ and its derivative vanish off $\Omega$, so those slab integrals equal their integrals over $\Omega$. Thus $\|\varphi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\le(b-a)^2\|\partial_e\varphi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\le(b-a)^2\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

cases.evidence: For the zero Sobolev function both the slab-width estimate and its gradient side vanish, including throughout the smooth approximation passage.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,
u)$ be finite measure spaces with masses $0<M_X:=\mu(X)<\infty$ and $0<M_Y:=
u(Y)<\infty$. Put $d\widehat\mu=d\mu/M_X$ and $d\widehat
u=d
u/M_Y$. For $a\in L^2(X	imes Y,\mu	imes
u)$, let $T_a:L^2(Y,
u)	o L^2(X,\mu)$ be its square-integrable-kernel operator and let $\widehat T$ be the operator with kernel $\widehat a:=\sqrt{M_XM_Y}\,a$ against $\widehat
u$. The maps $U_Xg=\sqrt{M_X}g$ and $U_Yh=\sqrt{M_Y}h$ are unitary and
$$U_XT_aU_Y^{-1}=\widehat T.$$
Moreover $\|\widehat a\|_{L^2(\widehat\mu	imes\widehat
u)}=\|a\|_{L^2(\mu	imes
u)}$, so the operator norms and kernel $L^2$ norms agree. If either mass is zero, the corresponding $L^2$ space and kernel operator are zero.

For $X=Y=D$ with Lebesgue mass $M>0$, the normalized kernel is $\widehat a=Ma$ and the measure is $d\widehat x=dx/M$.

2.1 For $g\in L^2(Y,\widehat
u)$, $U_Y^{-1}g=g/\sqrt{M_Y}$. Using $d
u=M_Yd\widehat
u$ in the integral defining $T_a$ and then multiplying the output by $\sqrt{M_X}$ gives $U_XT_aU_Y^{-1}g=\int_Y\sqrt{M_XM_Y}a(x,y)g(y)\,d\widehat
u(y)$. The equality holds almost everywhere by [F2], and is independent of representatives by [F1]. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Scaling both factors of the product measure gives $\|\widehat a\|_2^2=M_XM_Y\int|a|^2\,d(\widehat\mu\times\widehat\nu)=\int|a|^2\,d(\mu\times\nu)$. Unitary equivalence in step 2.1 therefore preserves the operator norm and the kernel $L^2$ norm. If either mass is zero, every $L^2$ class on that factor is zero, so the integral operator is zero. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $p\ge1$, the Legendre polynomial $P_p$ has exactly $p$ simple roots in $(-1,1)$, and $P_p'$ has exactly $p-1$ simple roots in $(-1,1)$, one between each consecutive pair of roots of $P_p$. Consequently, the $p+1$ nodes consisting of $-1$, $1$, and the roots of $P_p'$ are pairwise distinct.

1.1 Suppose $P_p$ has only $m<p$ sign-changing roots $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in $(-1,1)$ and set $q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-r_j)$, with $q=1$ if $m=0$. At each sign-changing root both $P_p$ and $q$ change sign, while at every other real root $P_p$ does not change sign; therefore $P_pq$ has one constant sign on $(-1,1)$ and is not identically zero. It is continuous and nonzero on some open interval, so its integral is nonzero. But $\deg q=m<p$, and [F2] gives $\int_{-1}^1P_pq=0$, a contradiction. Thus $P_p$ has at least $p$ sign-changing roots in the open interval. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 A degree-$p$ polynomial cannot have more than $p$ distinct roots. The $p$ roots obtained in step 1.1 therefore exhaust its degree; each has multiplicity one and there are no other roots. Rolle's theorem [F3] between consecutive roots gives $p-1$ distinct roots of $P_p'$ in $(-1,1)$. Since $P_p'$ has degree $p-1$, these are all its roots and each is simple. None equals an endpoint, so adjoining $-1$ and $1$ gives $p+1$ distinct nodes, including the case $p=1$ where there are no interior critical points. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $p\ge1$, the Legendre polynomial $P_p$ has exactly $p$ simple roots in $(-1,1)$, and $P_p'$ has exactly $p-1$ simple roots in $(-1,1)$, one between each consecutive pair of roots of $P_p$. Consequently, the $p+1$ nodes consisting of $-1$, $1$, and the roots of $P_p'$ are pairwise distinct.

1.1 Suppose $P_p$ has only $m<p$ sign-changing roots $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in $(-1,1)$ and set $q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-r_j)$, with $q=1$ if $m=0$. At each sign-changing root both $P_p$ and $q$ change sign, while at every other real root $P_p$ does not change sign; therefore $P_pq$ has one constant sign on $(-1,1)$ and is not identically zero. It is continuous and nonzero on some open interval, so its integral is nonzero. But $\deg q=m<p$, and [F2] gives $\int_{-1}^1P_pq=0$, a contradiction. Thus $P_p$ has at least $p$ sign-changing roots in the open interval. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 A degree-$p$ polynomial cannot have more than $p$ distinct roots. The $p$ roots obtained in step 1.1 therefore exhaust its degree; each has multiplicity one and there are no other roots. Rolle's theorem [F3] between consecutive roots gives $p-1$ distinct roots of $P_p'$ in $(-1,1)$. Since $P_p'$ has degree $p-1$, these are all its roots and each is simple. None equals an endpoint, so adjoining $-1$ and $1$ gives $p+1$ distinct nodes, including the case $p=1$ where there are no interior critical points. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

## Definition

Fix neutral point-source data $(A,V,\Lambda,\kappa_k,(x_i,q_i)_{i=1}^n)$ from
[[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]], an Ewald parameter
$\alpha>0$, integers $M_1,M_2,M_3\ge1$, an assignment order $P\ge2$, and write
$N_g=M_1M_2M_3$. Let $\mathcal G=\prod_{r=1}^3\{0,\ldots,M_r-1\}$ and take
$W_P$ from [[def-ewald-causal-cardinal-spline-window]]. Define the periodic
causal assignment weights, for $t\in[0,1)^3$ and $\ell\in\mathcal G$, by
$$w_\ell(t)=\prod_{r=1}^3\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z} W_P(M_rt_r-\ell_r-jM_r).$$
The sums are finite because $W_P$ is supported on $[0,P]$. They collect every
support index into its grid residue; if $P>M_r$, distinct support indices that
wrap to the same residue are added. The spread grid is
$$g_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n q_iw_\ell(t_i),\qquad t_i=A^{-1}x_i\pmod{\mathbb Z^3}.$$

Use the negative-sign unitary tensor DFT convention
$$\widehat g_M(k)=N_g^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}g_\ell e^{-2\pi i\sum_{r=1}^3k_r\ell_r/M_r},$$
which is the product transform of
[[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Signed frequency
representatives are chosen before evaluating windows. A retained set
$\mathcal K\subset\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ is finite, symmetric under
$k\mapsto-k$, injective modulo $(M_1,M_2,M_3)$, and satisfies
$|k_r|<M_r/2$ for each coordinate. In particular, even-grid Nyquist modes are
not silently retained.

For $u\in\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(u)/u$ when $u\ne0$ and
$\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$. Define
$$D(k)=\prod_{r=1}^3e^{-\pi iPk_r/M_r} \operatorname{sinc}(\pi k_r/M_r)^P.$$
Only modes with $D(k)\ne0$ are admissible for division. A computed
implementation must first certify a strictly positive lower bound for
$|D(k)|$; otherwise it returns `denominator-inconclusive` without dividing.
For $k\in\mathcal K$, define
$$a_k(t)=e^{-2\pi i k\cdot t},\quad b_k(t)=\frac{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t) e^{-2\pi i\sum_rk_r\ell_r/M_r}}{\overline{D(k)}},\quad \rho_k=\sum_iq_i a_k(t_i),\quad z_k=\frac{\sqrt{N_g}\,\widehat g_M(k)}{\overline{D(k)}}.$$
The denominator is the complex conjugate of the printed window multiplier; this
sign is part of the definition. Set
$$c_k=\frac{4\pi}{V|\kappa_k|^2} e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}.$$
The exact retained reciprocal energy is
$$E_{\mathcal K}=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|\rho_k|^2,$$
and the mesh reciprocal energy is
$$E_M=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|z_k|^2.$$

Let $\mathfrak d_k(t)$ be the declared physical mesh derivative: it is
$\nabla_xb_k(t)=A^{-T}\nabla_tb_k(t)$ wherever the classical derivative
exists. A grid knot is a point with $M_rt_r\in\mathbb Z$ for some coordinate
$r$. At a $P=2$ knot, take the one-sided vector limits from all adjacent open
mesh boxes. Define $\mathfrak d_k(t)$ to be any selected one-sided limit or the
arithmetic average of all those limits. This is a procedure value and does not
assert that the classical derivative exists there. The
energy-gradient mesh force is
$$F_{M,i}=-q_i\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\overline{z_k}\mathfrak d_k(t_i)\right).$$
Define the diagonal mesh-self correction and corrected reciprocal energy by
$$C_M=\frac12\sum_iq_i^2\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k (|b_k(t_i)|^2-1),\qquad E_M^{\mathrm{corr}}=E_M-C_M.$$
Whether the declared force is the derivative of this corrected energy, and the
error bound it satisfies, are proved separately.

## Definition

Use the data, quadtree and interaction decomposition of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]. Fix an expansion order $p\ge1$. If two different labels have the same position, return status `collision` before evaluating any singular interaction: the requested potential is undefined. Otherwise take as input a finite quadtree from the definition, together with its point-to-cell membership arrays and leaf threshold $s$. For $N=0$ return empty outputs. For $N\ge1$, construct $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ by the recursive decomposition in the definition. The tree and point-to-cell membership are preprocessing inputs; their construction is not part of the arithmetic passes below.

Using the supplied membership data, make a root-first list of nonempty cells: at each nonempty internal cell inspect its four children and recurse only into children $E$ with $I_E\ne\varnothing$; never descend into an empty subtree. Use the reverse list order for the bottom-up pass and the root-first order for the top-down pass. Use exact complex arithmetic throughout. For each nonempty leaf $C$ form the particle-to-multipole (P2M) moments
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n,\qquad 0\le n\le p.$$
For the upward multipole-to-multipole (M2M) pass, process nonempty internal cells bottom-up. For each such parent $C$ and each $0\le n\le p$, form its moments from its nonempty children by
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{\substack{E\text{ child of }C\\ I_E\ne\varnothing}}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E).$$
An empty child has zero moments and is skipped. Thus the upward pass visits only parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty.

## Statement

For every integer $\ell\ge0$, the space $\mathcal H_\ell$ of [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]] has dimension $2\ell+1$. For any orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell m}:-\ell\le m\le\ell\}$, there is a basis-independent normalized zonal polynomial $P_\ell$ such that
$$\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega')}=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega'),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$
It obeys $|P_\ell(t)|\le1$ for $-1\le t\le1$ and the generating identity
$$\frac1{\sqrt{1-2rt+r^2}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}r^\ell P_\ell(t),\qquad -1\le t\le1,\quad 0\le r<1.$$

## Statement

For every integer $\ell\ge0$, the space $\mathcal H_\ell$ of [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]] has dimension $2\ell+1$. For any orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell m}:-\ell\le m\le\ell\}$, there is a basis-independent normalized zonal polynomial $P_\ell$ such that
$$\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega')}=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega'),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$
It obeys $|P_\ell(t)|\le1$ for $-1\le t\le1$ and the generating identity
$$\frac1{\sqrt{1-2rt+r^2}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}r^\ell P_\ell(t),\qquad -1\le t\le1,\quad 0\le r<1.$$

2.1 Restriction of a homogeneous polynomial to $\mathbb S^2$ is injective, because homogeneity recovers its value at every nonzero $x$ from its value at $x/|x|$. Rank-nullity therefore gives $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=\binom{\ell+2}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}=2\ell+1$ for $\ell\ge2$, and direct counting gives $1$ and $3$ for $\ell=0,1$. Gram-Schmidt on any finite spanning list gives an orthonormal basis; no choice axiom is used. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix $\omega'$. After rotating it to the third coordinate axis, use $w=x_1+ix_2$ and $\bar w=x_1-ix_2$. A rotation sends these to $e^{i\theta}w$ and $e^{-i\theta}\bar w$, so an invariant monomial $w^a\bar w^b x_3^c$ must have $a=b$. The invariant homogeneous polynomials are therefore sums of $(x_1^2+x_2^2)^j x_3^{\ell-2j}$, whose restrictions to the sphere are polynomials $f(t)$ of degree at most $\ell$, with $t=x_3$. The polar-coordinate Laplacian is $\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$; applying it to $r^\ell f(\cos\theta)$ gives $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}f=-\ell(\ell+1)f$. For a zonal $f$, the angular term is $(\sin\theta)^{-1}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\partial_\theta f)=(1-t^2)f''-2tf'$ by $t=\cos\theta$, so $(1-t^2)f''-2tf'+\ell(\ell+1)f=0$. Writing $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}a_kt^k$ yields $(k+2)(k+1)a_{k+2}+\bigl(\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)\bigr)a_k=0$. For $\ell\ge1$, the equation at $k=\ell-1$, using $a_{\ell+1}=0$, gives $2\ell a_{\ell-1}=0$; descending through $k=\ell-3,\ell-5,\ldots$ forces every coefficient of parity opposite to $\ell$ to vanish. For $k=\ell-2,\ell-4,\ldots$, the coefficient $\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)$ is positive, so each lower coefficient of parity $\ell$ is determined by the next one. Thus the zonal solution space has dimension at most one (for $\ell=0$ it is the constants). The function $K_\ell(\cdot,\omega')$ is a zonal harmonic, and $K_\ell(\omega',\omega')=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)>0$, so a nonzero such solution exists. Define $P_\ell(t)=K_\ell(\omega,\omega')/K_\ell(\omega',\omega')$ when $t=\omega\cdot\omega'$. Rotation invariance makes this depend only on $t$, and $P_\ell(1)=1$. The diagonal value in step 3.1 now gives the displayed addition theorem. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

## Statement

For $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$ with $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the following necessary conditions hold.

If $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable, then $\operatorname{rank}[\lambda I-A\;B]=n$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely stabilizable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

If $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable, then $\operatorname{rank}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}=n$ for every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely detectable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

This proves the necessary half of the PBH tests. The converse pole-placement implication is not asserted here.

This proves the necessary half of the PBH tests. The converse pole-placement implication is not asserted here.

1.1 Suppose $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable and fix its same-field feedback $K$ from [F1]. If for some $\lambda$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$ the horizontal matrix $H_\lambda=[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$, [F2] and [F3] applied over $\mathbb C$ to $H_\lambda^*$ give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^n$ with $y^*(\lambda I-A)=0$ and $y^*B=0$. By [A1], the same real or complex $K$ acts on this vector, so $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting that $A-BK$ is Hurwitz. [A1, F1, F2, F3, contradiction]

1.2 Suppose $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable and fix its same-field injection $L$ from [F1]. If $V_\lambda=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}$ has rank less than $n$, rank-nullity over $\mathbb C$ gives a nonzero $x\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(\lambda I-A)x=0$ and $Cx=0$. Hence $(A-LC)x=\lambda x$, which contradicts that $A-LC$ is Hurwitz because $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. [A1, F1, F3, contradiction]

## Statement

For $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$ with $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the following necessary conditions hold.

If $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable, then $\operatorname{rank}[\lambda I-A\;B]=n$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely stabilizable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

If $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable, then $\operatorname{rank}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}=n$ for every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely detectable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

This proves the necessary half of the PBH tests. The converse pole-placement implication is not asserted here.

1.1 Suppose $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable and fix its same-field feedback $K$ from [F1]. If for some $\lambda$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$ the horizontal matrix $H_\lambda=[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$, [F2] and [F3] applied over $\mathbb C$ to $H_\lambda^*$ give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^n$ with $y^*(\lambda I-A)=0$ and $y^*B=0$. By [A1], the same real or complex $K$ acts on this vector, so $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting that $A-BK$ is Hurwitz. [A1, F1, F2, F3, contradiction]

2.1 Suppose $(A,B)$ is discretely stabilizable and fix its same-field Schur feedback $K$ from [F1]. If $[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$ for some $|\lambda|\ge1$, the same complex left-kernel argument as in step 1.1 gives a nonzero $y$ with $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting Schur stability. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, contradiction]

## Statement

Let $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$, $|z|<1$, and
$c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$. For the nonterminating Gauss-series term
$h_k=(a)_k(b)_kz^k/((c)_kk!)$, and any integer $N>|c|$,

$$\frac{|h_{k+1}|}{|h_k|} =|z|\frac{|a+k||b+k|}{|c+k|(k+1)} \le q_N:=|z|\frac{(1+|a|/N)(1+|b|/N)}{1-|c|/N} \qquad(k\ge N).$$

For sufficiently large $N$, $q_N<1$; then the tail starting at $h_N$ is at
most $|h_N|/(1-q_N)$. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, the series
terminates and its tail after the last nonzero term is zero.

1.1 For a nonzero term, the Pochhammer product gives $h_{k+1}/h_k=z(a+k)(b+k)/((c+k)(k+1))$. For $k\ge N>|c|$, $|a+k|\le k(1+|a|/N)$, $|b+k|\le k(1+|b|/N)$, $|c+k|\ge k(1-|c|/N)$, and $k+1\ge k$. These inequalities yield the stated $q_N$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 As $N\to\infty$, $q_N\to|z|<1$, so a finite $N$ has $q_N<1$; summing the geometric majorant proves the tail bound and local uniform convergence on compact subsets of $|z|<1$. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, its Pochhammer product becomes zero after finitely many terms, which proves the terminating case. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the map $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ of [[def-duffy-reference-triangle-map]], the image of $[0,1]^2$ is $T=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le1\}$. On $r>0$ it has inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y/x)$ and Jacobian determinant $r$; the edge $r=0$ maps to $(0,0)$.

1.1 For an increment $(h,k)$, $D(r+h,s+k)-D(r,s)=(h,sh+rk+hk)$. The linear part $(h,sh+rk)$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\s&r\end{pmatrix}$, while the remainder has Euclidean norm $|hk|\le(h^2+k^2)/2$; divided by $\|(h,k)\|_2=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ it tends to zero. Thus this is the total derivative. Its entries are continuous, so the polynomial extension is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ by [F2]; its determinant is $r$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $0\le r,s\le1$, then $0\le rs\le r\le1$, so $D(r,s)\in T$. Conversely, for $(x,y)\in T$ with $x>0$, $r=x$ and $s=y/x$ lie in $[0,1]$ and map to $(x,y)$; when $x=0$, $y=0$ and every $(0,s)$ maps to the vertex. For $r>0$, the displayed inverse is unique. This proves the image, inverse, and collapsed-edge claims. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix $\gamma>1$. In one space dimension the conserved state is
$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$, where $\rho$ is density, $m$ momentum, and
$E$ total energy per unit volume. The **admissible-state set** is the open set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>m^2/(2\rho)\}.$$
The ideal-gas pressure on this set is
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right)>0,$$
the velocity is $u=m/\rho$, and the flux is
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p,\frac{m}{\rho}(E+p)\right).$$
The sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. These definitions apply only
on $\mathcal G_\gamma$; a state with nonpositive density or nonpositive
internal energy is inadmissible. The set is open because $\rho$ and
$E-m^2/(2\rho)$ are continuous on $\rho>0$ and the inequalities are strict;
all displayed flux functions are smooth on this domain.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $G\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open connected set, and let $v\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(G;\mathbb R^3)$ have zero distributional curl. Every ball compactly contained in $G$ has an $H^1$ primitive of $v$. If every based loop in $G$ is homotopic to a constant loop fixing its basepoint, these local primitives glue to $f\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(G)$ with $\nabla f=v$. Such $f$ is unique up to a constant. This assertion alone does not assert global $L^2$ integrability of $f$ on $G$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $G\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open connected set, and let $v\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(G;\mathbb R^3)$ have zero distributional curl. Every ball compactly contained in $G$ has an $H^1$ primitive of $v$. If every based loop in $G$ is homotopic to a constant loop fixing its basepoint, these local primitives glue to $f\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(G)$ with $\nabla f=v$. Such $f$ is unique up to a constant. This assertion alone does not assert global $L^2$ integrability of $f$ on $G$.

2.1 Cover $G$ by its countable rational balls with compact closure in $G$, and choose the primitives in step 1.1. Every nonempty intersection of two such balls is convex and connected. By [F3], $g_B-g_C=c_{BC}$ almost everywhere on $B\cap C$, with a unique real constant; $c_{BC}=-c_{CB}$, and $c_{BC}+c_{CD}=c_{BD}$ whenever the triple intersection is nonempty. Consider a germ of a primitive to mean a local $H^1$ primitive on a neighborhood of a point, identifying two when they agree almost everywhere on a smaller neighborhood. Fix one germ at a basepoint. Along a path, choose a finite subdivision whose successive subpaths lie in balls, and transport the current primitive by adding the unique constant needed to agree on an overlap at each subdivision point. This defines the terminal germ. Inserting extra subdivision points does not change it, and changing the covering balls gives the same result: refine around every subdivision point so that all balls compared contain that point, use their nonempty open intersections, and use the displayed cocycle identity. Thus transport is well defined along a path and reverses under reversal of that path. [F3, step 1.1, construct, F5]

4.1 On a small ball around any point, path independence identifies these terminal germs with one fixed local primitive plus a constant. The resulting local functions therefore agree almost everywhere on overlaps. They define an $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ class on $G$: enumerate the countable ball cover and use the first applicable representative on each measurable difference of balls; the overlap exceptional sets have countable union of measure zero. Any compact subset has a finite ball subcover, so the class is $H^1$ locally, and its weak derivative is $v$ there and hence globally on compactly supported tests. This is $f$. Any two choices differ by a locally $H^1$ zero-gradient function, so [F3] makes the difference constant. AC is used only for the cited analytic interfaces and the countable local representative/primitive choices. [F3, step 3.1, construct, F4] ∎

This assertion alone does not assert global $L^2$ integrability of $f$ on $G$.

2.1 Cover $G$ by its countable rational balls with compact closure in $G$, and choose the primitives in step 1.1. Every nonempty intersection of two such balls is convex and connected. By [F3], $g_B-g_C=c_{BC}$ almost everywhere on $B\cap C$, with a unique real constant; $c_{BC}=-c_{CB}$, and $c_{BC}+c_{CD}=c_{BD}$ whenever the triple intersection is nonempty. Consider a germ of a primitive to mean a local $H^1$ primitive on a neighborhood of a point, identifying two when they agree almost everywhere on a smaller neighborhood. Fix one germ at a basepoint. Along a path, choose a finite subdivision whose successive subpaths lie in balls, and transport the current primitive by adding the unique constant needed to agree on an overlap at each subdivision point. Inserting extra subdivision points does not change it, and changing the covering balls gives the same result: refine around every subdivision point so that all balls compared contain that point, use their nonempty open intersections, and use the displayed cocycle identity. Thus transport is well defined along a path and reverses under reversal of that path. [F3, step 1.1, construct, F5]

3.1 Transport is invariant under endpoint-fixed path homotopy. For a continuous homotopy $H:[0,1]^2\to G$, compactness gives a finite subcover of its image by the ball cover and a Lebesgue number for the pullback cover of the square. A sufficiently fine rectangular grid then maps every closed cell into one ball. The transport around the boundary of that cell is the identity: compute it with that one ball's primitive; subdivision and ball independence from step 2.1 permit this computation. Compose these identities over all cells. Every interior edge is traversed once in each direction, so its transports cancel. The two vertical boundary paths are constant when endpoints are fixed; hence the transports along the two horizontal paths agree. If $G$ has the stated loop property, any two paths from the basepoint to a given point have equal terminal germs by applying this argument to their concatenation with one reversed. A connected open subset of Euclidean space is path connected: the set reachable by polygonal paths is both open and relatively closed, since a ball about any point joins that point to all nearby points. Thus there is a terminal germ at every point. [step 2.1, construct, algebra, F5]

## Definition

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;
3. the associated time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step
   $\delta_k\to0$.

The convergence in clause 2 and density of $V$ in $H$ imply
$\Pi_kz\to z$ in $H$ for every $z\in H$: use
$\|\Pi_k(z-v)\|_H\le\|z-v\|_H$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $H$, and approximate $z$
by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

For a fixed $k$, backward Euler with averages $f_k^n$ uses unknowns
$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Its piecewise-constant reconstruction is $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$(t_{n-1},t_n]$; its affine reconstruction joins $U_k^{n-1}$ to $U_k^n$.

cases.review_reason: The projections preserve zero, and both piecewise constant and affine reconstructions of zero discrete coefficients vanish; no division by a solution norm is introduced.

## Definition

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;

   $\delta_k\to0$.

by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations

Assume the Axiom of Choice and assume every connected edge component of the finite metric graph $\Gamma$
has at least one anchor in $D$. Put

$$\|w\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le L_\Gamma \left(\sum_{e\in E}\|w'_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

## Definition

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\ge1$. A **regular simplicial companion family** consists of refining uniformly regular boundary-anchored cell-face meshes in [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]], and, for each mesh, a matching simplicial subdivision $\mathcal S_h$ of its cells with the following finite geometric data and uniform constants $c,C,J>0$.

Each cell is subdivided into at most $J$ closed nondegenerate $d$-simplices. Each simplex has diameter at most $Ch$ and inradius at least $ch$, and the chosen cell point $x_K$ is a subdivision vertex. The subdivision of each cell is a fan from $x_K$ over a triangulation of its boundary, and subdivisions agree on shared faces. Each original face is a union of at most $J$ subdivision facets. In dimension one these mean the two subintervals from $x_K$ to the endpoints.

For each subdivision vertex $z$, let $\mathcal K(z)$ consist of the original cells whose closures contain $z$. This set has at most $J$ elements. For any $K,L\in\mathcal K(z)$ there is a path of at most $J$ cells in $\mathcal K(z)$, from $K$ to $L$, consecutive cells sharing an original face whose closure contains $z$. If $z\in\partial\Omega$, every $K\in\mathcal K(z)$ has such a path to a cell with a boundary face whose closure contains $z$. These are connectivity checks on finite vertex stars, not an assumption of an analytic inequality.

For shared face values $v_F$, cell values $v_K$, and homogeneous boundary values $v_F=0$, define the piecewise constant state $\Pi_hv|_K=v_K$ and
$$D_{h,p}(v)^p=\sum_K\sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|d_{K,F}^{1-p}|v_F-v_K|^p\qquad(1<p<\infty).$$
The mean interpolator $I_hv$ has cell and face values equal to the corresponding means of a Sobolev function, with face means interpreted by the simplex trace; for $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ its boundary face means are zero. Define $E_hv$ to be continuous and affine on each subdivision simplex, with nodal value $|\mathcal K(z)|^{-1}\sum_{K\in\mathcal K(z)}v_K$ at an interior vertex $z$ and zero at a boundary vertex. Thus $E_h$ is an explicit linear function of the cell values; its definition does not assume its stability.

These conditions allow nonorthogonal cells. A nonempty example in every dimension is the uniform cubical partition of $(0,1)^d$, with cell centers, a fixed matching barycentric subdivision of every face, and the cones from cell centers to those face simplices. Scaling leaves finitely many simplex shapes and bounded vertex stars; coordinate adjacency connects each interior star and connects each boundary star to a boundary face. In dimension one use equal subintervals and their midpoints. Hence all the displayed constants can be chosen independently of refinement.

## Definition

Let $\mathcal T$ be a cell-face mesh as in [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]], with $x_K$ the volume centroid of each cell and $x_F$ the face centroid. For the mimetic branch require the following explicit face-moment closure on each cell:
$$ \sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|n_{K,F}=0,\qquad \sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|x_F\otimes n_{K,F}=|K|I_d. $$
Here $I_d$ is the identity matrix on $\mathbb R^d$ and $(x\otimes n)_{ij}=x_i n_j$. These are finite geometric checks on the face data; they impose no center-to-face orthogonality. For every cell use one real cell-mean unknown $u_K$; for every face use one shared real face-mean unknown $u_F$. On a boundary face $F\subset\partial\Omega$, the value $u_F=g_F$ is prescribed. Write $n_{K,F}$ for the outward unit normal. Define the reconstructed cell gradient and its face residual by
$$ G_Ku=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|u_Fn_{K,F},\qquad \rho_{K,F}(u)=u_F-u_K-G_Ku\cdot(x_F-x_K). $$
Interpret $u_K$ and $u_F$ as cell and face averages. For a symmetric positive-definite tensor $A_K$ constant on $K$ (so $z\cdot A_Kz>0$ for every nonzero $z$), define
$$ \mathscr A_K(u,v)=|K|(A_KG_Ku)\cdot G_Kv+\lambda_{\min}(A_K)\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{|F|}{d_{K,F}}\rho_{K,F}(u)\rho_{K,F}(v), $$
where $\lambda_{\min}(A_K)>0$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $A_K$. The **linear hybrid mimetic scheme** with homogeneous Dirichlet data is to find all cell and interior-face values $u$ such that
$$ \sum_{K\in\mathcal K}\mathscr A_K(u,v)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal K}v_K\int_K f(x)\,dx $$
for every test vector $v$ whose boundary face values are zero. For each local face $F\subset\partial K$, let $\phi_{K,F}$ have face value $1$ on $F$, zero on the other faces of $K$, and cell value zero. Define the outward numerical flux $Q_{K,F}(u)=-\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_{K,F})$.

There is also a monotone $p$-growth backward-Euler extension, specified as an algebraic scheme but with no existence or convergence claim in this definition. Let $1<p<\infty$, set $p'=p/(p-1)$, and let $a(x,\xi)$ be a **Carathéodory flux**, meaning that $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable for each fixed $\xi$ and $\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous for almost every $x$. Assume there are constants $C,\alpha>0$, a nonnegative $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$, and a nonnegative $h\in L^1(\Omega)$ such that, outside one null set,
$$ |a(x,\xi)|\le C(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),\qquad (a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0. $$
For each cell set $b_K(\xi)=|K|^{-1}\int_Ka(x,\xi)\,dx$, and fix $\alpha_{0,K}>0$. Put $\psi_p(s)=|s|^{p-2}s$ for $s\ne0$ and $\psi_p(0)=0$. Its spatial operator, linear in the test vector $v$, is
$$ \mathcal A_{h,K}(u;v)=|K|b_K(G_Ku)\cdot G_Kv+\alpha_{0,K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{|F|}{d_{K,F}^{p-1}}\psi_p(\rho_{K,F}(u))\rho_{K,F}(v). $$
For this extension define $Q_{K,F}^{\rm nl}(u)=-\mathcal A_{h,K}(u;\phi_{K,F})$.
On a time partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, given $u^{n-1}$ and $f\in L^{p'}((0,T)\times\Omega)$, put $f_K^n=((t_n-t_{n-1})|K|)^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}\int_K f$. The backward-Euler step seeks $u^n$ with zero boundary face values satisfying
$$ \sum_{K\in\mathcal K}|K|\frac{u_K^n-u_K^{n-1}}{t_n-t_{n-1}}v_K+\sum_{K\in\mathcal K}\mathcal A_{h,K}(u^n;v)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal K}|K|f_K^n v_K $$
for every test vector with zero boundary face values. The formula specifies a candidate discrete method; solvability and convergence require separate results.

For an affine function $\ell(x)=b\cdot x+c$, its cell and face averages satisfy $G_K\ell=b$ and $\rho_{K,F}(\ell)=0$ by the displayed face-moment closure. The drawing illustrates the cell and face degrees of freedom on a skew cell; no center-to-face orthogonality is assumed.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1]
  \draw[thick] (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (3,1) -- (1,1) -- cycle;
  \fill (1.5,0.5) circle (2pt) node[below] {$u_K$};
  \fill (1,0) circle (2pt) node[below] {$u_{F_1}$};
  \fill (2.5,0.5) circle (2pt) node[right] {$u_{F_2}$};
  \fill (2,1) circle (2pt) node[above] {$u_{F_3}$};
  \fill (0.5,0.5) circle (2pt) node[left] {$u_{F_4}$};
  \draw[->,blue] (1.5,0.5) -- (2.2,0.5) node[right] {$G_Ku$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

When $p=2$, $b_K(\xi)=A_K\xi$, and $\alpha_{0,K}=\lambda_{\min}(A_K)$, the nonlinear formula agrees with the linear form above. Neither specification by itself proves solvability, a conforming $W_0^{1,p}$ reconstruction, or a mesh-uniform discrete Aubin–Lions estimate; those require separate results or hypotheses.

## Definition

Let $\mathcal T$ be a cell-face mesh as in [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]], with $x_K$ the volume centroid of each cell and $x_F$ the face centroid. For the mimetic branch require the following explicit face-moment closure on each cell:
$$ \sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|n_{K,F}=0,\qquad \sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|x_F\otimes n_{K,F}=|K|I_d. $$
Here $I_d$ is the identity matrix on $\mathbb R^d$ and $(x\otimes n)_{ij}=x_i n_j$. These are finite geometric checks on the face data; they impose no center-to-face orthogonality. For every cell use one real cell-mean unknown $u_K$; for every face use one shared real face-mean unknown $u_F$. On a boundary face $F\subset\partial\Omega$, the value $u_F=g_F$ is prescribed. Write $n_{K,F}$ for the outward unit normal. Define the reconstructed cell gradient and its face residual by
$$ G_Ku=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}|F|u_Fn_{K,F},\qquad \rho_{K,F}(u)=u_F-u_K-G_Ku\cdot(x_F-x_K). $$
Interpret $u_K$ and $u_F$ as cell and face averages. For a symmetric positive-definite tensor $A_K$ constant on $K$ (so $z\cdot A_Kz>0$ for every nonzero $z$), define
$$ \mathscr A_K(u,v)=|K|(A_KG_Ku)\cdot G_Kv+\lambda_{\min}(A_K)\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{|F|}{d_{K,F}}\rho_{K,F}(u)\rho_{K,F}(v), $$
where $\lambda_{\min}(A_K)>0$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $A_K$. The **linear hybrid mimetic scheme** with homogeneous Dirichlet data is to find all cell and interior-face values $u$ such that
$$ \sum_{K\in\mathcal K}\mathscr A_K(u,v)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal K}v_K\int_K f(x)\,dx $$
for every test vector $v$ whose boundary face values are zero. For each local face $F\subset\partial K$, let $\phi_{K,F}$ have face value $1$ on $F$, zero on the other faces of $K$, and cell value zero. Define the outward numerical flux $Q_{K,F}(u)=-\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_{K,F})$.

There is also a monotone $p$-growth backward-Euler extension, specified as an algebraic scheme but with no existence or convergence claim in this definition. Assume there are constants $C,\alpha>0$, a nonnegative $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$, and a nonnegative $h\in L^1(\Omega)$ such that, outside one null set,
$$ |a(x,\xi)|\le C(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),\qquad (a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0. $$

## Example

For $0<\delta<1$, set $\lambda:=3(1-\delta)$, define
$$ (Ku)(x):=\lambda x\int_0^1 yu(y)\,dy,$$
and let $f(x)=1$. The exact solution of $u-Ku=f$ is
$$u(x)=1+\frac{\lambda}{2\delta}x.$$
For the $N$-panel composite midpoint rule with $h=1/N$, the Nyström solution is
$$u_N(x)=1+\frac{\lambda}{2(\delta+\lambda h^2/12)}x.$$
Its error is the midpoint residual multiplied by a factor
$$(\delta+\lambda h^2/12)^{-1},$$
which is at least $(2\delta)^{-1}$ whenever $\lambda h^2/12\le\delta$.
Thus a small quadrature residual can produce a much larger solution error as
$\delta$ approaches the resonance value $0$.

## Statement

Use the spaces and operators of
[[def-na-periodic-staggered-grid-stokes-operators]] with $d\ge1$, $N\ge2$,
and $h=1/N$. Then $\Delta_h=D_hG_h$ maps $Q_h$ bijectively to itself, the
kernel of $\Delta_h$ on all cell arrays consists exactly of the constants,
and $D_hv$ has zero mean for every $v\in V_h$. In addition, every $q\in Q_h$
satisfies the resolution-independent bound
$$ \|q\|_{Q_h}\le\sqrt d\,\|G_hq\|_{M_h}. $$

1.2 Let $q\in Q_h$. Since $q$ has mean zero, $$ q_x=N^{-d}\sum_{y\in J_N}(q_x-q_y), $$ and [F3]–[F4] give the finite-sum Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $$ \|q\|_{Q_h}^2\le N^{-2d}\sum_{x,y\in J_N}|q_x-q_y|^2. $$ For each ordered pair $(x,y)$ choose the path that changes coordinates in the order $1,\ldots,d$, moving forward modulo $N$ in each coordinate. It has at most $dN$ directed edges. Cauchy--Schwarz along the path bounds $|q_x-q_y|^2$ by $dN$ times the sum of squared edge differences on it. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

5.1 Fix one directed edge in coordinate $i$. For each coordinate $r<i$, its value along the path is $y_r$; to use the fixed edge, $y_r$ is fixed and $x_r$ has at most $N$ choices. For each $r>i$, the path still has value $x_r$; then $x_r$ is fixed and $y_r$ has at most $N$ choices. In coordinate $i$ there are at most $N^2$ ordered start/end pairs. Hence this edge occurs in at most $N^{d+1}$ paths. Summing the path bounds and dividing by $N^{2d}$ yields $$ \|q\|_{Q_h}^2\le dN^{2-d}\sum_{i,j}|q_{j+e_i}-q_j|^2 =d\|G_hq\|_{M_h}^2. $$ Taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated inequality. ## Definition

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral
domain with a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T$. Here
Lipschitz polyhedral means that the boundary is a finite union of flat
simplex faces and, near each boundary point after a rigid coordinate change,
$\Omega$ lies on one side of a Lipschitz graph. Let $\mathcal F^\circ$ and
$\mathcal F^\partial$ be its interior and boundary facets. For a cellwise
affine function $v$, write $v_K$ for its polynomial restriction to $K$. The
broken gradient $\nabla_hv$ is defined by $(\nabla_hv)|_K:=\nabla v_K$.
For a facet $F$ and an integrable function $w$ on $F$, let $h_F:=\operatorname{diam}(F)$ and write $\operatorname{avg}_F(w):=|F|^{-1}\int_Fw\,dS$.
The homogeneous Crouzeix–Raviart space is
$$V_h^{CR,0}:=\left\{v\in L^2(\Omega): v_K\in\mathbb P_1(K)\ \text{for each }K\in\mathcal T,\quad \int_F(v_{K^+}-v_{K^-})\,dS=0\ \text{for }F=K^+\cap K^-\in\mathcal F^\circ,\quad \int_Fv_K\,dS=0\ \text{for }F\in\mathcal F^\partial\right\}.$$
The ordering $K^+,K^-$ on an interior facet is arbitrary; the zero-mean
condition is independent of that ordering. The functions need not agree
pointwise on a facet and need not belong to $H^1(\Omega)$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nondegenerate affine simplex, let $F$ be one of its facets, and let $s>1/2$. Restriction of smooth functions has a unique bounded extension
$$T_F:H^s(K)\longrightarrow L^2(F),\qquad \|T_Fv\|_{L^2(F)}\le C_s\|v\|_{H^s(K)},$$
where $H^s(K)$ is the restriction space of [[def-nitsche-restriction-bessel-potential-sobolev-spaces]]. The constant depends only on $s$ and the Fourier normalization, not on the location or orientation of the supporting hyperplane. If $V\in H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ is an extension of $v$, then $T_Fv$ is the restriction to $F$ of the unique $L^2$ hyperplane trace of $V$; hence it is independent of the chosen extension.

Write $J_F=\det DF$, and assume $j_-\le J_F\le j_+$ and $\|DF\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|DF^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L$ almost everywhere on the cells. For every $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, its pullback $\widehat u=u\circ F$ lies in $H^1(\widehat\Omega)$, with cellwise weak gradient
$$\nabla_\xi\widehat u=DF^\mathsf T(\nabla_xu)\circ F.$$
The inverse pullback also preserves $H^1$, and
$$\|\widehat u\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}\le j_-^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)},\qquad \|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le j_+^{1/2}\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\|\widehat u\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}.$$
Pullback maps $H^1_0(\Omega)$ onto $H^1_0(\widehat\Omega)$. For a vector field $\widehat v=v\circ F$, the physical gradient is $(\nabla_\xi\widehat v)DF^{-1}$, so the scalar diffusion and finite-Lamé elasticity forms are transformed by the same Jacobian and inverse-map factors.

abla_\xi(v\circ F)=DF^\mathsf T(
abla_xv)\circ F$. Fix a test function compactly supported in $\widehat\Omega$. Its support stays away from the exterior patch boundary. On every part of a cell where the test function is nonzero, its image under $F$ lies in a compact subset of $\Omega$, so $v\circ F$ and its first derivatives are bounded there; near exterior faces the test function vanishes. Apply the divergence theorem [F6] to $(v\circ F)\phi e_j$ cell by cell. The values of $v\circ F$ and $\phi$ agree on either side of every shared face, so opposite normal fluxes cancel, and exterior terms vanish. This proves the weak-derivative identity without requiring $v$ to extend to $\partial\Omega$. Cellwise change of variables [F2], summed over the finite partition using finite additivity of the integral, yields $\|v\circ F\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)}^2\le j_-^{-1}\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,\qquad \|
abla_\xi(v\circ F)\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)}^2\le L^2j_-^{-1}\|
abla_xv\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$ Thus $\|v\circ F\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}\le j_-^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+L^2}\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. The same argument applied to $F^{-1}$, whose Jacobian is $J_F^{-1}$ and derivative is bounded by $L$, gives the reverse estimate. [F2, F3, F6, given, algebra]

## Statement

Let $m\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty compact, let $v:K\to\mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous (so $\limsup_{y\to x}v(y)\le v(x)$ for each $x\in K$), and extend $v$ by $-\infty$ off $K$. For $\lambda>0$ define
$$\widehat v(\xi)=\max_{x\in K}\{v(x)-\tfrac\lambda2|x-\xi|^2\}.$$
This is finite, continuous and $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R^m$, meaning that $\widehat v(\xi)+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ is convex ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]). If $(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}\widehat v(\eta)$, every maximizing point equals $y=\eta+q/\lambda$, and
$$(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}v(y),\qquad v(y)=\widehat v(\eta)+\frac{|q|^2}{2\lambda}.$$
The jets of $v$ are understood for its extended function, or for its original local domain if $y$ is interior to $K$. These conclusions use no choice principle.

## Statement

Let $m\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty compact, let $v:K\to\mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous (so $\limsup_{y\to x}v(y)\le v(x)$ for each $x\in K$), and extend $v$ by $-\infty$ off $K$. For $\lambda>0$ define
$$\widehat v(\xi)=\max_{x\in K}\{v(x)-\tfrac\lambda2|x-\xi|^2\}.$$
This is finite, continuous and $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R^m$, meaning that $\widehat v(\xi)+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ is convex ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]). If $(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}\widehat v(\eta)$, every maximizing point equals $y=\eta+q/\lambda$, and
$$(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}v(y),\qquad v(y)=\widehat v(\eta)+\frac{|q|^2}{2\lambda}.$$
The jets of $v$ are understood for its extended function, or for its original local domain if $y$ is interior to $K$. These conclusions use no choice principle.

1.1 The maximum exists by [F1], is finite above by $\max_K v$, and is finite below by evaluating at any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Expanding the square gives $\widehat v(\xi)+\lambda|\xi|^2/2=\sup_{x\in K}\{v(x)-\lambda|x|^2/2+\lambda x\cdot\xi\}$. Every expression in the supremum is affine in $\xi$, so the supremum is convex; finiteness and [F2] give continuity and the asserted semiconvexity. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix a maximizer $y$ at $\eta$. Evaluation at $y$ and the upper-jet inequality [F3] give, for small $h$, $\lambda(y-\eta)\cdot h-\lambda|h|^2/2\le\widehat v(\eta+h)-\widehat v(\eta)\le q\cdot h+h^{\mathsf T}Yh/2+o(|h|^2)$. Put $h=te$ for every unit $e$ and both signs of $t$, divide by $|t|$, and let $t\to0$; then $\lambda(y-\eta)=q$, so the maximizer is unique and the value identity follows. For $x$ near $y$, set $\xi=\eta+x-y$, so the penalty is unchanged; the same jet inequality gives $v(x)-v(y)\le\widehat v(\eta+x-y)-\widehat v(\eta)\le q\cdot(x-y)+(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Y(x-y)/2+o(|x-y|^2)$. This is the transferred upper jet, and for an interior $y$ the extension and original function agree locally. [step 1.1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, $m,n\ge0$, $f\in C(I,\mathbb R)$, and a strictly
positive continuous weight $w$, there is $r_*\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ such
that
$$\|w(f-r_*)\|_{\infty,I}=E_{m,n}(f,w;I).$$

3.2 For the minimizing pair, $q_*$ is a nonzero nonnegative polynomial because its coefficient norm is $1$. Its zero set in $I$ is finite by [F4]. The defining inequality of $K$ and $w\ge\gamma$ give $|p_*(x)|\le(\|f\|_{\infty,I}+M/\gamma)q_*(x)$ for every $x\in I$. At any zero $c$ of $q_*$, repeated use of [F5] writes $q_*(x)=(x-c)^s u(x)$ with $u(c)
e0$ and, if $p_*
e0$, writes $p_*(x)=(x-c)^r v(x)$ with $v(c)
e0$. If $p_*
e0$ and $r<s$, then [F8] and [F4] give $q_*(x)>0$ on a punctured one-sided neighborhood of $c$ inside $I$. By continuity in [F6] and $u(c)v(c)
e0$, $|v(x)|/|u(x)|$ is bounded below by a positive constant on a sufficiently small such neighborhood, so $|p_*(x)|/q_*(x)=|x-c|^{r-s}|v(x)|/|u(x)|$ is unbounded as $x	o c$ from within $I$, contradicting the displayed bound. Hence $p_*$ is divisible by the factor of $q_*$ at every interval zero; this is automatic if $p_*=0$. Thus every interval zero of $q_*$ cancels from the quotient. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F8, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each interior zero $c$ of $q_*$, its multiplicity is even: an odd multiplicity would make $q_*$ change sign across $c$, contradicting $q_*\ge0$ on $I$. Form $H$ from the factors $(x-c)^s$ at interior zeros (where $s$ is even), $(x-a)^{s_a}$ at $a$ if it is a zero, and $(b-x)^{s_b}$ at $b$ if it is a zero. Then $H\ge0$ on $I$ and $H>0$ off the finite zero set of $q_*$. Step 3.2 shows that $H$ divides both $p_*$ and $q_*$. Write $p_*=H\bar p$ and $q_*=H\bar q$. The exact multiplicities included in $H$ make $\bar q$ nonzero at every zero of $q_*$; elsewhere, $q_*>0$ and $H>0$, so $\bar q>0$. Since $\bar q$ is continuous by [F6], positivity off the finite zero set makes it nonnegative at each removed zero; its nonvanishing there makes it positive on all of $I$. At every point outside those zeros, divide the defining inequality $|w(fq_*-p_*)|\le t_*q_*$ by $H$ to obtain $|w(f\bar q-\bar p)|\le t_*\bar q$. Thus $|w(f-\bar p/\bar q)|\le t_*$ there. The quotient $\bar p/\bar q$ and $w(f-\cdot)$ are continuous on $I$ by [F6], so the same bound holds at the cancelled zeros by continuity. Reduce $(\bar p,\bar q)$ using [F2]. The reduced denominator still has no zero on $I$ because it divides $\bar q$; it is continuous by [F6] and has constant sign by [F9] (otherwise the intermediate value theorem would give a zero). A common sign change makes it positive, and a further positive scaling gives coefficient norm $1$. The resulting pair is admissible and represents the same quotient, hence has error at most $t_*$. Therefore $E_{m,n}(f,w;I)\le t_*$. Together with step 3.1, equality holds and the infimum is attained. [F1, F2, F6, F9, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement
Let $d\ge1$, $\tau_r>0$, and integers $M_r,w_r\ge1$ satisfy $M_r\ge2w_r+1$. Define $a_r=\pi/(\tau_rM_r^2)$ and
$$S_r=\frac{2}{1-\exp(-a_r)},\qquad T_r=2\exp(-a_rw_r^2)\left(1+\frac{1}{2a_rw_r}\right).$$
For $x=(x_r)_{r=1}^d\in[0,1)^d$, let
$$W_r(x_r)=\left\{\ell\in\{0,\ldots,M_r-1\}:\min_{n\in\mathbb Z}|\ell/M_r-x_r-n|\le w_r/M_r\right\},\quad W(x)=\prod_{r=1}^dW_r(x_r).$$
With $\Phi_\tau(z)=\prod_{r=1}^d\phi_{\tau_r}(z_r)$, the omitted spreading mass obeys
$$\sum_{\ell\in\prod_r\{0,\ldots,M_r-1\}\setminus W(x)}\Phi_\tau(\ell_1/M_1-x_1,\ldots,\ell_d/M_d-x_d)\le T_d,\qquad T_d:=\sum_{r=1}^dT_r\prod_{s\ne r}S_s.$$
Also $\sum_{\ell_r=0}^{M_r-1}\phi_{\tau_r}(\ell_r/M_r-x_r)\le S_r$ for every coordinate and point.

1.2 If $\ell\notin W_r(x_r)$, then every $m=\ell+nM$ satisfies $|m-y|>w$. On either side of $y$, the lattice distances form a unit-spaced sequence $d+n$ with $d>w$. The first term is at most $\exp(-aw^2)$. For each later term, monotonicity of $f_a$ gives $f_a(d+n)\le\int_{d+n-1}^{d+n}f_a(t)\,dt$. For $R>w$, [F3]–[F4] give $\int_w^R f_a(t)\,dt\le\frac1w\int_w^Rt f_a(t)\,dt=\frac{\exp(-aw^2)-\exp(-aR^2)}{2aw}\le\frac{\exp(-aw^2)}{2aw}.$ By [F5], the last subtracted term tends to zero as $R\to\infty$. Taking limits of the finite tail sums, which converge by [F1], bounds each side by $\exp(-aw^2)(1+1/(2aw))$. Both sides together yield $\sum_{\ell\notin W_r(x_r)}\phi_\tau(\ell/M-x_r)\le T_r$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 The complement of the product set $W(x)$ is the union of the $d$ sets where at least one coordinate index is outside its $W_r(x_r)$. Since all kernel terms are nonnegative, the total omitted product mass is at most the sum of the $d$ coordinate-tail product sums. Each such finite product factors into the one-coordinate tail in step 1.2 and the full-coordinate masses in step 1.1; hence it is at most $T_r\prod_{s\ne r}S_s$. Summing over $r$ gives $T_d$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, $R=R^*\succ0$, and $Q=C^*C$. Assume $(A,B)$ is discretely stabilizable and $(A,C)$ discretely detectable, using [[def-lqr-stabilizability-and-detectability]]. Then the DARE of [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]] has exactly one Hermitian positive-semidefinite solution $X$. ## Statement

For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, let $\ell_+(z)$ be the branch in
[[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]]. Define
$$\Phi(u)=\int_0^u\bigl(\lfloor v\rfloor-v+1/2\bigr)\,dv.$$
Then the absolutely convergent integral satisfies
$$\ell_+(z)=\left(z-\frac12\right)\operatorname{Log}z-z+ \frac12\log(2\pi)+\int_0^\infty\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du.$$
On each unit interval, $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$ for $0\le t\le1$; hence
$0\le\Phi(u)\le1/8$.

## Statement

For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, let $\ell_+(z)$ be the branch in
[[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]]. Define
$$\Phi(u)=\int_0^u\bigl(\lfloor v\rfloor-v+1/2\bigr)\,dv.$$
Then the absolutely convergent integral satisfies
$$\ell_+(z)=\left(z-\frac12\right)\operatorname{Log}z-z+ \frac12\log(2\pi)+\int_0^\infty\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du.$$
On each unit interval, $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$ for $0\le t\le1$; hence
$0\le\Phi(u)\le1/8$.

1.1 Define $f(u)=\lfloor u\rfloor-u+1/2$. For $u=n+t$ with integer $n\ge0$ and $0\le t<1$, $f(u)=1/2-t$. Each full unit interval has integral zero, and its partial integral is $t(1-t)/2$. Therefore $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$, $\Phi(n)=0$, and $0\le\Phi\le1/8$. [given, F7, algebra]

2.2 On each $[n,n+1]$, write $f(u)=n+\tfrac12-u=(n+z+\tfrac12)-(u+z)$. By [F5] the function $(n+z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(u+z)-u$ has derivative $f(u)/(u+z)$; its derivative is continuous and integrable on the compact interval by [F6]. Applying [F6] and summing the resulting endpoint differences yields $$I_N(z)=(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) -(z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z-N-\log((N-1)!) -zH_{N-1}+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\left(\frac zk-\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)\right).$$ The coefficient of each internal $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)$ in the endpoint sum is $-1$. For $k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)=\log k+\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)$ because $k>0$ is real and multiplication by it preserves the principal argument; [F9] gives $\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\log k=\log((N-1)!)$. These identities give the displayed form. [given, F5, F6, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

For every $z\in\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, the value $\ell(z)$ in
[[def-loggamma-slit-plane-branch]] is independent of the integer $m\ge0$ with
$\operatorname{Re}(z+m)>0$, is holomorphic on $\Omega$, and satisfies
$e^{\ell(z)}=\Gamma(z)$.

1.1 For $\operatorname{Re}w>0$, the function $H(w)=\ell_+(w+1)-\ell_+(w)-\operatorname{Log}w$ is holomorphic by [F1], and $e^{H(w)}=1$ by [F1] and [F2]. Differentiating this identity by [F5] gives $e^{H(w)}H'(w)=0$, hence $H'(w)=0$ since $e^{H(w)}=1$. By [F6], $H$ is constant on the connected right half-plane. For positive real $w$, all three terms are real, so that constant is $0$. Therefore $\ell_+(w+1)=\ell_+(w)+\operatorname{Log}w$ throughout the right half-plane. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, $E\ne\varnothing$, and that the anchor set $D$ meets every connected
edge component of the finite metric graph $\Gamma$. Let constant edge
diffusivities satisfy
$$0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_e\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty.$$
For every $f\in H=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R)$ there is a unique
$u\in V_D$ such that

$$a(u,v):=\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e=F(v):=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}f_ev_e\,dx_e\qquad(v\in V_D).$$

The equation is the anchored weak metric-graph diffusion problem. Whenever
$u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$ as defined in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], the Green identity
[[lem-metric-graph-kirchhoff-green-identity]] identifies its interior
equation as $-\kappa_eu''_e=f_e$ and its natural free-vertex condition as
Kirchhoff balance of the outward diffusive fluxes.

## Definition

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron, or a periodic rectangular cell. The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

## Statement

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite boundary-anchored TPFA mesh and let $T_e>0$ be its interior and boundary transmissibilities. A **boundary path family** assigns to each cell $K$ a finite simple path $\gamma_K$ of adjacent interior faces, followed by one boundary face of its terminal cell; simple means it visits no cell more than once. Set $\Delta_eu=u_K-u_L$ on an interior face $e=K|L$ with a fixed orientation, and set $\Delta_eu=u_K$ on a boundary face of $K$. The sign of an interior increment is reversed when the path traverses the fixed orientation backward. Put
$$ S_K=\sum_{e\in\gamma_K}T_e^{-1},\qquad C_{\rm path}=\max_{e}\sum_{K:e\in\gamma_K}|K|S_K. $$
Then every cell vector $u$ satisfies the discrete Poincaré inequality
$$ \sum_{K\in\mathcal K}|K|u_K^2\le C_{\rm path}\sum_{e}T_e(\Delta_eu)^2=C_{\rm path}\|u\|_{E_h}^2. $$
Consequently, any uniformly regular mesh family supplied with boundary path families whose $C_{\rm path}$ are uniformly bounded has a mesh-uniform Poincaré constant. This theorem does not assert that every orthogonal mesh family has such a uniform path bound.

## Statement

For W from [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]] and coordinate indices j,k,l,

$$\int \partial_kW(z)\,dz=0,\qquad \int z_j\partial_kW(z)\,dz=-\delta_{jk},\qquad \int z_jz_l\partial_kW(z)\,dz=0.$$

Also m₃=∫|z|³|∇W(z)|dz is finite.

1.1 Choose a box with the support of W in its interior. Every integrand below is continuous on this box by [F1] and integrable by [F5]. Fix all coordinates except z_k. Applying [F4] with F=W and G=1 gives ∫∂_kW dz_k=0 because W vanishes near the two endpoints. Applying it with G=z_j gives ∫z_j∂_kW dz_k=−δ_{jk}∫W dz_k. Integrating the section identities over the remaining coordinates by [F3] gives the first identity and ∫z_j∂_kW dz=−δ_{jk}∫W dz=−δ_{jk}. [F1, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 With G=z_jz_l, [F4] gives ∫z_jz_l∂_kW dz=−δ_{jk}∫z_lW dz−δ_{lk}∫z_jW dz after [F3] integrates the other coordinates. Both moments vanish by [F2]. Finally |z|³|∇W| is continuous and compactly supported, so [F5] makes its integral finite; this is m₃. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1] ∎

Assume AC and let $a:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. For $K$ and $K_n$
from [[def-half-order-product-integration]], put $A:=\|a\|_\infty$ and

$$w_{n,j}(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^n|w_{n,j}(x)|  =2\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{1-x}\le2\sqrt2$$

function on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$ and

$$\|K_nu-Ku\|_\infty\le\frac{\sqrt2}{4}M_2h^2.$$

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $k:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $K$ its integral
operator, and $K_N$ its composite midpoint Nyström operator with panel width
$h=1/N$. Suppose $I-K$ is injective and $u$ solves $(I-K)u=f$. Assume that
$g_x(y):=k(x,y)u(y)$ is twice continuously differentiable in $y$ for every
$x$, with the uniform bound
$$M_2:=\sup_{x,y\in[0,1]}|\partial_y^2g_x(y)|<\infty.$$
Then there are $N_0$ and $C<\infty$ such that for every $N\ge N_0$ the Nyström
matrix is nonsingular, its reconstruction $u_N$ solving $(I-K_N)u_N=f_N$
exists for each $f_N\in X$, and
$$\|u_N-u\|_\infty\le C\left(\|f_N-f\|_\infty+\frac{h^2}{24}M_2\right).$$
In the standard Nyström method $f_N=f$. The regularity assumption is on the
actual function $k(x,\cdot)u(\cdot)$, not on every function in the unit ball of
$C([0,1],\mathbb R)$.

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses and Schur bounds of
[[thm-na-pressure-schur-spectral-equivalence-from-infsup]], with constants
$\alpha,\Lambda,C_b,\beta>0$. For $\gamma>0$, use
$P_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(A,\gamma M_Q)$ from
[[def-na-symmetric-saddle-point-system-and-block-preconditioners]], and set
$$ a_\gamma=\frac{\beta^2}{\Lambda\gamma},\qquad b_\gamma=\frac{C_b^2}{\alpha\gamma},\qquad \lambda_\pm(s)=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4s}}2. $$
Let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m$ be the eigenvalues, with multiplicity, of
$(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}S(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}$. Then
$a_\gamma\le\mu_j\le b_\gamma$, and the symmetric square-root-preconditioned
saddle matrix has eigenvalues
$$ \{\lambda_-(\mu_j),\lambda_+(\mu_j):1\le j\le m\} \quad\text{and }1\text{ with multiplicity }n-m. $$
Consequently its spectrum is contained in
$$ [\lambda_-(b_\gamma),\lambda_-(a_\gamma)]\;\cup\; \{1\}\;\cup\; [\lambda_+(a_\gamma),\lambda_+(b_\gamma)], $$
where the eigenvalue $1$ has multiplicity zero if $n=m$. This is a spectral
estimate for the stated scaled block preconditioner, not an iteration-count
or generic solver-speed claim.

3.1 The matrix $TT^T$ is positive definite by step 1.1, so for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$, $x=T^T(TT^T)^{-1}y$ satisfies $Tx=y$. Thus $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is onto, and [F4] gives $\dim\ker T=n-m$. For $x\in\ker T$, $X(x,0)=(x,0)$, giving eigenvalue $1$ on this kernel. The $m$ orthonormal pairs from step 2.1 and this $n-m$ dimensional kernel account for all $n+m$ dimensions and hence for the full spectrum of $X$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $C$ is the Cholesky factor in the symmetric-preconditioning definition, then $P_\gamma=CC^T$. Let $O=P_\gamma^{-1/2}C$; step 1.1 gives $OO^T=I$, so $O$ is orthogonal and $$ C^{-1}KC^{-T}=O^T(P_\gamma^{-1/2}KP_\gamma^{-1/2})O. $$ Therefore the published Cholesky-symmetric preconditioning has the same spectrum as $X$. Since $\lambda_-$ decreases and $\lambda_+$ increases on $s>0$, the eigenvalue intervals follow from step 1.1. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

$$\Pi_hv|_T=|T|^{-1}\int_Tv\,ds.$$
There is a family-independent constant $C$ such that
$$\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\qquad(v\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)).$$
If $\lambda$ is continuously differentiable on each planar face (with facewise derivatives square integrable), then
$$\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{3/2}\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}.$$
Here $\nabla_\Gamma\lambda$ is the ordinary two-dimensional gradient on each planar face; no continuity of these derivatives across edges is assumed.

$$\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\qquad(v\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)).$$

1.2 For facewise $C^1$ $\lambda$, apply [F2] on each planar triangle, which is convex, to obtain $\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(T)}$. Squaring and summing yields $\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le Ch\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}$. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $e=\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda$. For any $w\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, [F3] gives $\int_Te\,ds=0$, hence $\int_\Gamma ew\,ds=\sum_T\int_Te(w-w_T)\,ds.$ Cauchy–Schwarz over the finite element sum, step 1.2 for $e$, and step 1.1 for $w$ give $|\langle e,w\rangle|\le \|e\|_{L^2}\|w-\Pi_hw\|_{L^2}\le Ch^{3/2}\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}.$ Taking the supremum over $\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}\le1$ proves the negative-half-order estimate. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the $C^2$ boundary and orientation of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]], there are bounded traces from either side of a bounded collar into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, bounded trace lifts into $H^1(\Omega^-)$ and into compactly supported $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and bounded extensions of the classical layers
$$S_k:H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3),\qquad D_k:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1(\Omega^-)\oplus H^1_{\rm loc}(\overline{\Omega^+}).$$
Here the exterior local space means $H^1$ on each bounded exterior collar/domain truncation, including its boundary. Both restrictions solve $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ weakly and have bounded weak conormals in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. With the fixed normal $n$, they obey Green's identity, with duality linear in the conormal and conjugate-linear in the trace. Their exterior restrictions are smooth away from $\Gamma$ and satisfy the uniform Sommerfeld condition $\sup_\omega|r(\partial_r-ik)u(r\omega)|\to0$. Bounds are at fixed $k$ and fixed bounded neighborhoods. The single layer has one trace across $\Gamma$.

1.1 Write $a(\xi)=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. For a compactly supported smooth flat-space function $v$, Fourier inversion in the last coordinate and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|\widehat{v(\cdot,0)}(\xi)|^2\le C a(\xi)^{-1}\int(a(\xi)^2+4\pi^2\tau^2)|\widehat v(\xi,\tau)|^2d\tau$. Integration in $\xi$ proves the flat $H^1\to H^{1/2}$ trace estimate. The lift $\widehat{Lg}(\xi,t)=\widehat g(\xi)e^{-a(\xi)|t|}\chi(t)$, with $\chi=1$ near zero and compactly supported, has trace $g$ and $H^1$ norm bounded by $C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$, by integrating $e^{-2a|t|}$. In a $C^2$ graph chart $x=(z,t+\psi(z))$, the change of variables has determinant one and bounded derivative and inverse derivative; the chain rule bounds the two $H^1$ norms. Graph and chart distances and surface Jacobians are uniformly comparable, so the Slobodeckij double integral gives the corresponding $H^{1/2}$ norm comparison. A finite partition of unity and smaller chart cutoffs therefore transport the flat trace and lifts to the surface. For each bounded physical chart piece and flat half-box use [F92]. A $C^2$ graph map has bounded derivative, inverse derivative and Jacobian, so the classical chain rule and change of variables bound composition on smooth approximants; passing their functions and derivatives in $L^2$ gives the weak composition formula and $H^1$ convergence for all inputs. This proves the one-sided trace/extension passage without assuming smoothness of an arbitrary Sobolev representative. For the normal-coordinate identity, smooth approximants from [F92] satisfy the classical one-variable FTC. Their traces converge by the flat trace estimate, and their normal-derivative integrals converge in tangential $L^2$, uniformly over a bounded normal interval, by Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking these limits supplies the $L^2$ slice representative and its integral identity for every normal parameter. A zero-trace $H^1$ function then has zero-extension in $H^1$ (the distributional boundary derivative is its trace times $n$, which vanishes), and the kernel of the trace is $H^1_0$: in a flat half-chart a zero-trace function satisfies $v(z,t)=\int_0^t\partial_tv(z,s)ds$, whence $\epsilon^{-2}\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|v|^2\le C\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|\partial_tv|^2\to0$. Cutting it off for $t<\epsilon$ therefore changes its $H^1$ norm by a quantity tending to zero; convolution of each resulting interior-supported function proves the claim. Transport this construction by the graph maps and sum the partition.
