Integration in $\xi$ proves the flat $H^1\to H^{1/2}$ trace estimate. The lift $\widehat{Lg}(\xi,t)=\widehat g(\xi)e^{-a(\xi)|t|}\chi(t)$, with $\chi=1$ near zero and compactly supported, has trace $g$ and $H^1$ norm bounded by $C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$, by integrating $e^{-2a|t|}$. In a $C^2$ graph chart $x=(z,t+\psi(z))$, the change of variables has determinant one and bounded derivative and inverse derivative; the chain rule bounds the two $H^1$ norms. Graph and chart distances and surface Jacobians are uniformly comparable, so the Slobodeckij double integral gives the corresponding $H^{1/2}$ norm comparison. A finite partition of unity and smaller chart cutoffs therefore transport the flat trace and lifts to the surface. For each bounded physical chart piece and flat half-box use [F92]. A $C^2$ graph map has bounded derivative, inverse derivative and Jacobian, so the classical chain rule and change of variables bound composition on smooth approximants; passing their functions and derivatives in $L^2$ gives the weak composition formula and $H^1$ convergence for all inputs. This proves the one-sided trace/extension passage without assuming smoothness of an arbitrary Sobolev representative. For the normal-coordinate identity, smooth approximants from [F92] satisfy the classical one-variable FTC. Their traces converge by the flat trace estimate, and their normal-derivative integrals converge in tangential $L^2$, uniformly over a bounded normal interval, by Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking these limits supplies the $L^2$ slice representative and its integral identity for every normal parameter. A zero-trace $H^1$ function then has zero-extension in $H^1$ (the distributional boundary derivative is its trace times $n$, which vanishes), and the kernel of the trace is $H^1_0$: in a flat half-chart a zero-trace function satisfies $v(z,t)=\int_0^t\partial_tv(z,s)ds$, whence $\epsilon^{-2}\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|v|^2\le C\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|\partial_tv|^2\to0$. Transport this construction by the graph maps and sum the partition. In a $C^2$ graph chart, the map $(z,t)\mapsto\Phi(z)+tn_{\Phi(z)}$ is $C^1$ and at $t=0$ its tangent columns and unit-normal column are linearly independent. The Euclidean inverse-function theorem gives a local normal collar with bounded derivative, inverse derivative and Jacobian after shrinking to a compact subchart; a finite cover provides the required fixed bounds; transporting this estimate proves $L^2$ convergence of the normal slices to the Sobolev trace from either side. These arguments apply to $C^2$ charts directly and do not import any polyhedral trace theorem. To verify density of the declared ambient smooth densities in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, lift any chart datum by the constructed compactly supported global $H^1$ lift, mollify that lift in $H^1$ as in [F92], and apply the bounded trace estimate: the traces of the smooth approximants converge in the chart norm. They are also dense in $L^2(\Gamma)$ by chart cutoffs and ordinary mollification. Their density in $H^{-1/2}$ follows by Hilbert duality: an annihilator in $H^{1/2}$ would have zero $L^2$ pairing with every such density and hence be zero; Riesz identifies the dual of the negative space with the positive space. [F1, F92, F93, given, algebra, construct]

4.1 Given $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, take a bounded interior lift $F_0$ from step 1.1. On $H^1_0(\Omega^-)$ apply [F2] to $b(v,w)=\int(\nabla v\cdot\overline{\nabla w}+v\bar w)$ and the functional $-b(F_0,w)$. This produces $F=F_0+v$ with trace $\phi$, $(-\Delta+1)F=0$, and $\|F\|_{H^1}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}$. Define $q\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ by $\langle q,g\rangle=b(F,Lg)$ for an interior lift $Lg$. Independence follows since differences of lifts are in $H^1_0$, and boundedness follows from step 1.1. For $f=F1_{\Omega^-}$ and any smooth compactly supported test $v$, two weak integrations by parts give $P_kf(v)=-(1+k^2)\int_{\Omega^-}Fv+q(v|_\Gamma)-\int_\Gamma\phi\partial_nv$. In distributions, the last term is minus the source of the classical double layer. Convolving this equality with $G_k$ is legitimate because $f$ has compact support, and $G_k*P_kf=(P_kG_k)*f=f$. Consequently define $D_k\phi=S_kq-(1+k^2)G_k*f-f.$ For smooth $\phi$, the differentiated fundamental-solution identity and distributional convolution identify this expression away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\phi(y)dS_y$. The first term is $H^1$ near $\Gamma$, the second is $H^2$ by step 2.1, and $f$ restricts to $F$ and zero on the two sides. This proves the asserted bounded piecewise $H^1$ extension and its uniqueness by density. It also shows its trace jump is $-\phi$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

For positions $X_1,\ldots,X_P\in\mathbb T_L^d$ and real charges $q_1,\ldots,q_P$, define $Q=\sum_pq_p$ and an admissible algebraic assignment shape $w_j$ as in [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]]. Then
$$ h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}h^{-d}\sum_{p=1}^Pq_pw_j(X_p)=Q . $$
Consequently the neutralized source $\rho_j(X)=h^{-d}\sum_pq_pw_j(X_p)-Q/L^d$ has mean zero and is in the range of the periodic Poisson operator; it therefore has a unique mean-zero potential for the gauge $\bar\phi=0$ by [[thm-periodic-centered-difference-poisson-zero-mode-and-gauge]].

1.1 Before subtracting the background, sum the assigned density with cell volume. Since the sum is finite, interchange its particle and grid sums; [F2] gives $h^d\sum_j h^{-d}\sum_pq_pw_j(X_p)=\sum_pq_p\sum_jw_j(X_p)=\sum_pq_p=Q .$ [given, F1, F2, algebra]
3.1 By [F3], this zero-mean source has a solution and fixing its mean to zero selects exactly one potential. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge0$, $c_j\in\mathbb C$, $x_j\in[0,1)^d$, integers $K_r\ge0$, positive integers $M_r>2K_r$, and $\tau_r>0$. Write $P=\prod_{r=1}^dM_r$, define $\Phi_\tau(z)=\prod_{r=1}^d\phi_{\tau_r}(z_r)$, and let
$$g_\ell=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\Phi_\tau(\ell_1/M_1-x_{j,1},\ldots,\ell_d/M_d-x_{j,d}),\quad 0\le\ell_r<M_r.$$
For $k\in\mathcal K=\prod_r\{-K_r,\ldots,K_r\}$ define the normalized grid DFT
$$\widetilde g_k=\frac1P\sum_{\ell_1=0}^{M_1-1}\cdots\sum_{\ell_d=0}^{M_d-1}g_\ell\exp\!\left(-2\pi i\sum_{r=1}^d k_r\ell_r/M_r\right).$$
Put $\widehat\Phi(m)=\prod_r\sqrt{\tau_r}\exp(-\pi\tau_r m_r^2)$. Then
$$\widetilde g_k=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z^d}\widehat\Phi(k+q\odot M)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\exp(-2\pi i(k+q\odot M)\cdot x_j),$$
where $(q\odot M)_r=q_rM_r$. In particular, $\widehat\Phi(k)>0$ and
$$\frac{\widetilde g_k}{\widehat\Phi(k)}=F_k+\sum_{q\ne0}\left[\prod_{r=1}^d\exp\!\left(-\pi\tau_r((k_r+q_rM_r)^2-k_r^2)\right)\right]\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\exp(-2\pi i(k+q\odot M)\cdot x_j).$$
For $s_r=\exp(-\pi\tau_rM_r(M_r-2K_r))\in(0,1)$ and
$$A=\prod_{r=1}^d\left(1+\frac{2s_r}{1-s_r}\right)-1,$$
the alias error satisfies
$$\left|\frac{\widetilde g_k}{\widehat\Phi(k)}-F_k\right|\le A\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|c_j|.$$

1.1 Substitute [F1] into each factor of $\Phi_\tau$ and then into $\widetilde g_k$. Absolute uniform convergence in [F1] permits interchanging the finite grid/source sums with the absolutely convergent Fourier series. For an integer $m_r$, the coordinate root sum is $\frac1{M_r}\sum_{\ell_r=0}^{M_r-1}e^{2\pi i(m_r-k_r)\ell_r/M_r}=\begin{cases}1,&m_r-k_r\in M_r\mathbb Z,\\0,&m_r-k_r\notin M_r\mathbb Z.\end{cases}$ Indeed, in the first case every term is $1$; in the second, $z=e^{2\pi i(m_r-k_r)/M_r}\ne1$ by [F3] while $z^{M_r}=1$, so the finite geometric sum is $(1-z^{M_r})/(1-z)=0$. Thus only $m_r=k_r+q_rM_r$ remain in each coordinate, giving the displayed exact alias identity. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Since $M_r>2K_r$, $\tau_r>0$ and $\pi>0$ by [F6], the exponent parameter $\lambda_r=\pi\tau_rM_r(M_r-2K_r)$ is positive. Positivity and strict monotonicity of $\exp$ in [F6] imply $0<s_r=e^{-\lambda_r}<1$. Fix one coordinate $r$. If $q_r=\pm h$ with integer $h\ge1$ and $|k_r|\le K_r$, then $(k_r+q_rM_r)^2-k_r^2=q_r^2M_r^2+2q_rM_rk_r\ge h^2M_r^2-2hM_rK_r\ge hM_r(M_r-2K_r)>0.$ Hence the absolute alias multiplier for that coordinate is at most $s_r^h$. By [F5] its sum over nonzero $q_r$ is at most $2s_r/(1-s_r)$, so the sum over all coordinate multi-indices other than zero is at most the product of the coordinate sums including their unit terms, minus the all-zero term, namely $A$. The unit-modulus fact [F4], multiplicativity, and the triangle inequality in [F7] bound each source phase sum by $\sum_j|c_j|$. This gives the asserted alias bound. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge0$, $c_j\in\mathbb C$, $x_j\in[0,1)^d$, integers $K_r\ge0$, positive integers $M_r>2K_r$, and $\tau_r>0$. Write $P=\prod_{r=1}^dM_r$, define $\Phi_\tau(z)=\prod_{r=1}^d\phi_{\tau_r}(z_r)$, and let
$$g_\ell=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\Phi_\tau(\ell_1/M_1-x_{j,1},\ldots,\ell_d/M_d-x_{j,d}),\quad 0\le\ell_r<M_r.$$
For $k\in\mathcal K=\prod_r\{-K_r,\ldots,K_r\}$ define the normalized grid DFT
$$\widetilde g_k=\frac1P\sum_{\ell_1=0}^{M_1-1}\cdots\sum_{\ell_d=0}^{M_d-1}g_\ell\exp\!\left(-2\pi i\sum_{r=1}^d k_r\ell_r/M_r\right).$$
Put $\widehat\Phi(m)=\prod_r\sqrt{\tau_r}\exp(-\pi\tau_r m_r^2)$. Then
$$\widetilde g_k=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z^d}\widehat\Phi(k+q\odot M)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\exp(-2\pi i(k+q\odot M)\cdot x_j),$$
where $(q\odot M)_r=q_rM_r$. In particular, $\widehat\Phi(k)>0$ and
$$\frac{\widetilde g_k}{\widehat\Phi(k)}=F_k+\sum_{q\ne0}\left[\prod_{r=1}^d\exp\!\left(-\pi\tau_r((k_r+q_rM_r)^2-k_r^2)\right)\right]\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\exp(-2\pi i(k+q\odot M)\cdot x_j).$$
For $s_r=\exp(-\pi\tau_rM_r(M_r-2K_r))\in(0,1)$ and
$$A=\prod_{r=1}^d\left(1+\frac{2s_r}{1-s_r}\right)-1,$$
the alias error satisfies
$$\left|\frac{\widetilde g_k}{\widehat\Phi(k)}-F_k\right|\le A\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|c_j|.$$

## Statement

Let $T_n=(t_{i-j})_{0\le i,j<n}$ be Hermitian positive definite, and let $b\in\mathbb C^n$. Run [[alg-hermitian-toeplitz-general-rhs-gohberg-semencul-solve]] in exact arithmetic. It returns $x=T_n^{-1}b$. If $u=T_n^{-1}e_0$ and $v=T_n^{-1}e_{n-1}$ are the first and last inverse columns, then
$$T_n^{-1}=\frac1{u_0}\left(L(u)L(u)^*-L(Z_nv)L(Z_nv)^*\right),\qquad u_0>0.$$
The recursion and four triangular Toeplitz products use $O(n^2)$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ storage beyond the input, output, and lag vector. This is an exact-arithmetic cost statement and makes no finite-precision stability claim.

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$, $d\ge2$, and let $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ denote its cut-$k$ unfolding. For sequential TT-SVD, let $r_k$ be its retained bond size and $\delta_k$ its discarded singular-value tail at cut $k$. For rounding, let the input TT represent $A$ and use the same notation for the output bond sizes and recorded tails. Then both procedures satisfy
$$ \|A-\widehat A\|_F^2\le\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\delta_k^2. $$
If no positive singular value is discarded, the output is exactly $A$. In full-rank TT-SVD, $r_k=\operatorname{rank}(A^{\langle k\rangle})$ for every cut, and these are the minimal possible TT bond sizes among exact representations.

1.2 For rounding, let $C_\ell$ be the contraction of cores $\ell+1,\ldots,d$, with row index the bond after core $\ell$ and column index the suffix $(i_{\ell+1},\ldots,i_d)$; the empty suffix gives $C_d=[1]$. Put $R_\ell=C_\ell^*$. Backward induction from $C_d$ shows $C_\ell C_\ell^*=I$: if $G_{\ell+1}^{(R)}$ is the right matricization of core $G_{\ell+1}$ and $C_{\ell+1}C_{\ell+1}^*=I$, then $C_\ell=G_{\ell+1}^{(R)}(I_{n_{\ell+1}}\otimes C_{\ell+1})$, so $C_\ell C_\ell^*=G_{\ell+1}^{(R)}(I_{n_{\ell+1}}\otimes C_{\ell+1}C_{\ell+1}^*)G_{\ell+1}^{(R)*}=G_{\ell+1}^{(R)}G_{\ell+1}^{(R)*}=I$ by right-isometry. Forward induction similarly gives orthonormal columns for each prefix interface: $L_0=[1]$ and $L_j=(L_{j-1}\otimes I_{n_j})G_j^{(L)}$. Since $L_{j-1}^*L_{j-1}=I$, $(L_{j-1}\otimes I_{n_j})^*(L_{j-1}\otimes I_{n_j})=I$, so $L_j^*L_j=G_j^{(L)*}G_j^{(L)}=I$. When the right-to-left sweep processes cut $k$, cores $1,\ldots,k$ still have that left gauge and cores $k+2,\ldots,d$ have the right gauge. The current cut unfolding is $L_kM_{k+1}J$, where $M_{k+1}$ is core $G_{k+1}$ reshaped with row index the incoming bond and column index $(i_{k+1},\alpha_{k+1})$, and $J=I_{n_{k+1}}\otimes R_{k+1}^*$. Since $R_{k+1}^*R_{k+1}=I$, $JJ^*=I$. The local SVD truncation replaces $M_{k+1}$ by $M_{k+1}V_qV_q^*$, where $V_q$ has the retained right singular vectors, so the full unfolding changes from $L_kM_{k+1}J$ to $L_kM_{k+1}V_qV_q^*J=(L_kM_{k+1}J)(J^*V_qV_q^*J)$. Since $JJ^*=I$ and $V_q^*V_q=I$, $J^*V_qV_q^*J$ is the orthogonal projection onto $T_k=\operatorname{ran}(J^*V_q)$, a subspace of the suffix modes $k+1,\ldots,d$. Thus the resulting tensor is the projection onto $S_k=\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_k}\otimes T_k$. With $E=M_{k+1}(I-V_qV_q^*)$, the global residual norm satisfies $\|L_kEJ\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(J^*E^*L_k^*L_kEJ)=\operatorname{tr}(E^*EJJ^*)=\|E\|_F^2=\delta_k^2$. At the next cut $k-1$, the right interface $R_k$ has orthonormal columns spanning $T_k$. Its local embedding is $I_{n_k}\otimes R_k$, so every newly retained suffix vector lies in $\operatorname{ran}(I_{n_k}\otimes R_k)=\mathbb F^{n_k}\otimes T_k$. Hence $S_{k-1}\subseteq S_k$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

4.1 In either algorithm, let $A_0=A$ and let $A_j$ be the approximation after the $j$th truncation in execution order. By steps 3.1 and 1.2, each step is an orthogonal projection onto a retained subspace nested inside the preceding one. Therefore $e_j=A_{j-1}-A_j$ is orthogonal to every later increment, which lies in the retained subspace at step $j$. Telescoping gives $A-\widehat A=\sum_j e_j$, an orthogonal sum, and each $\|e_j\|_F$ is the recorded tail for that cut. Hence $\|A-\widehat A\|_F^2=\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\delta_k^2$. If a zero-rank truncation occurs, the output becomes zero and the unperformed tails are zero, so this same argument includes that branch. If no positive singular value is discarded, every $\delta_k=0$ and the output is exactly $A$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $e_2=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}$, $M=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1/50)$, and $D_1=D_2=(3/50)e_2e_2^*$. The exact sum $A=M+D_1+D_2=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/10)$ is positive definite. If each rank-one update is separately recompressed to rank zero with tolerance $\delta=3/50$ before assembly, both local truncations are accepted and the assembled approximation is $M$, which is indefinite. Each local error $3/50$ is below the smaller diagonal coefficient $1/10$ of $A$. The example concerns truncation of low-rank updates before their sum is assembled; it does not claim that every SVD truncation of a completed positive-definite H-matrix destroys positivity.

## Statement

Let $\widehat X=\widehat X^*$ be a DARE candidate, $S(X)=R+B^*XB$, $K(X)=S(X)^{-1}B^*XA$, $A_c(X)=A-BK(X)$, and let
$$F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB S(X)^{-1}B^*XA-X.$$
Suppose $S(\widehat X)\succeq\delta_0I$ is outward-certified. For a proposed radius $\rho>0$ put
$$a=\|A\|_2,\quad b=\|B\|_2,\quad m=\|\widehat X\|_F+\rho,\quad \delta=\delta_0-b^2\rho.$$
Require $\delta>0$ and define
$$L_K=\frac{ab}{\delta}+\frac{ab^3m}{\delta^2},\quad M_c=a+\frac{ab^2m}{\delta},\quad L_c=bL_K,\quad L_D=2M_cL_c.$$
Let $D(E)=A_c(\widehat X)^*EA_c(\widehat X)-E$ be invertible on Hermitian matrices, with outward-certified $\kappa\ge\|D^{-1}\|_{F\to F}$ and $r\ge\|F_d(\widehat X)\|_F$. If
$$\kappa(r+L_D\rho^2/2)\le\rho,\qquad \kappa L_D\rho<1,$$
there is exactly one Hermitian DARE root in the closed Frobenius $\rho$-ball, and $R+B^*XB\succeq\delta I$ throughout that ball.

For the stabilizing branch, additionally suppose $\widehat A_c=A_c(\widehat X)$ is Schur stable and an outward-certified $W\succ0$ satisfies
$$W-\widehat A_c^*W\widehat A_c\succeq\gamma I.$$
If, with $\eta=L_c\rho$,
$$\|W\|_2(2M_c\eta+\eta^2)<\gamma,$$
then the root is Schur-stabilizing. Under the standard DARE hypotheses of [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], it is the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution.

$$\kappa(r+L_D\rho^2/2)\le\rho,\qquad \kappa L_D\rho<1,$$
there is exactly one Hermitian DARE root in the closed Frobenius $\rho$-ball, and $R+B^*XB\succeq\delta I$ throughout that ball.

For the stabilizing branch, additionally suppose $\widehat A_c=A_c(\widehat X)$ is Schur stable and an outward-certified $W\succ0$ satisfies
$$W-\widehat A_c^*W\widehat A_c\succeq\gamma I.$$
If, with $\eta=L_c\rho$,
$$\|W\|_2(2M_c\eta+\eta^2)<\gamma,$$
then the root is Schur-stabilizing. Under the standard DARE hypotheses of [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], it is the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution.

1.1 For any Hermitian $E$ with $\|E\|_F\le\rho$, [F3] and [F4] give $S(\widehat X+E)=S(\widehat X)+B^*EB\succeq(\delta_0-b^2\rho)I=\delta I.$ Thus $S(X)$ is invertible on the ball and $\|S(X)^{-1}\|_2\le\delta^{-1}$. The resolvent identity gives $\|S(X)^{-1}-S(Y)^{-1}\|_2\le b^2\delta^{-2}\|X-Y\|_F.$ Using $K(X)=S(X)^{-1}B^*XA$ and splitting the difference into the change in $X$ and the change in $S^{-1}$ yields $\|K(X)-K(Y)\|_F\le L_K\|X-Y\|_F,\qquad \|A_c(X)\|_2\le M_c,\quad \|A_c(X)-A_c(Y)\|_2\le L_c\|X-Y\|_F.$ [F1, A1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 The root equation is the fixed-point equation $E=\mathcal T(E):=-D^{-1}F_d(\widehat X)-D^{-1}R(E).$ The assumptions make $\mathcal T$ a self-map of the closed ball. For $E,F$ in that ball, integrating $D_X-D$ along the segment between them gives $\|R(E)-R(F)\|_F\le L_D\rho\|E-F\|_F,$ so $\mathcal T$ has contraction factor at most $\kappa L_D\rho<1$. Iteration from zero has successive differences bounded by a geometric sequence, hence is Cauchy. The closed Hermitian ball is complete by [F8], so the sequence converges in the ball; continuity makes its limit a fixed point. The same contraction inequality makes it unique. [A1, F2, F8, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 The root equation is the fixed-point equation $E=\mathcal T(E):=-D^{-1}F_d(\widehat X)-D^{-1}R(E).$ The assumptions make $\mathcal T$ a self-map of the closed ball. The closed Hermitian ball is complete by [F8], so the sequence converges in the ball; continuity makes its limit a fixed point. The same contraction inequality makes it unique. [A1, F2, F8, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $X=\widehat X+E$ be the root. Then $\|A_c(X)-\widehat A_c\|_2\le L_c\rho=\eta$. Expanding the Stein form, $A_c(X)^*WA_c(X)-\widehat A_c^*W\widehat A_c=\widehat A_c^*W\Delta+\Delta^*W\widehat A_c+\Delta^*W\Delta,$ where $\Delta=A_c(X)-\widehat A_c$. Its norm is at most $\|W\|_2(2M_c\eta+\eta^2)<\gamma$. Hence $W-A_c(X)^*WA_c(X)\succ0$. For an eigenvector $A_c(X)v=\lambda v$, this gives $(1-|\lambda|^2)v^*Wv>0$, so $|\lambda|<1$. Let $K=K(X)$, $S=R+B^*XB$, and $x_{k+1}=A_c(X)x_k$, $u_k=-Kx_k$. Since $SK=B^*XA$, we have $K^*SK=A^*XB S^{-1}B^*XA$. Expanding $A_c^*XA_c=(A-BK)^*X(A-BK)$ gives $A_c^*XA_c=A^*XA-K^*SK-K^*SK+K^*B^*XBK=A^*XA-K^*SK-K^*RK.$ The DARE root equation therefore gives $X=Q+K^*RK+A_c^*XA_c$, which along $x_{k+1}=A_c x_k$ and $u_k=-Kx_k$ is the exact square identity $x_k^*Qx_k+u_k^*Ru_k+x_{k+1}^*Xx_{k+1}=x_k^*Xx_k.$ Summing to $N-1$ yields $x_0^*Xx_0=\sum_{k<N}(x_k^*Qx_k+u_k^*Ru_k)+x_N^*Xx_N$. By [F7], $x_N\to0$, so $x_0^*Xx_0$ is a sum of nonnegative terms; hence $X\succeq0$. Now [F6] identifies it as the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution. [A1, F1, F6, F7, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$, and let $\alpha,\beta>-1$. Let $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}$ be the finite positive Borel measure with density $(1-t)^\alpha(1+t)^\beta$ on $(-1,1)$ from [[lem-gauss-jacobi-weight-finite-moment-measure]]. Its moments through degree $2n-1$ are finite and its support is all of $[-1,1]$, so it is Gaussian moment data of order $2n-1$ in [[def-gauss-moment-data]]. The **$n$-node Gauss–Jacobi rule** is the general Gaussian rule $Q_n$ for this measure as defined in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]: its nodes are the roots of the monic degree-$n$ orthogonal polynomial, and each weight is the integral of the corresponding Lagrange cardinal polynomial. This definition makes no accuracy or computed-node claim; local well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-gauss-jacobi-rule-data-well-defined]].

## Example

Work in nondimensional coordinates with $u(x)=x^2+x^3$ and reconstruct the face $x=0$, the interface between cells $I_{-1}$ and $I_0$. This is a first-order critical point: $u'(0)=0$ and $u''(0)=2$. If the WENO-JS parameter is scaled as $\epsilon_h=h^4$, the cell-average face state has error $\frac{54}{95}h^4+O(h^5)$, so this branch is fourth order at the face. With the fixed $\epsilon_0>0$ of [[thm-na-weno-js-fixed-epsilon-fifth-order-reconstruction]], the theorem's fifth-order branch applies; with the same $\epsilon_h$, the WENO-Z comparison has error $O(h^6)$ on this polynomial.

1.1 Differentiate P using the finite-sum rule [F3]. The self terms vanish because ∇W_ε(0)=0 by [F2], and grouping the remaining terms by unordered pairs gives Ṗ=Σ_{i<j}(F_ij+F_ji)=0. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Differentiate J using the coordinatewise product rule [F3]; the terms v_i⊗v_i cancel, leaving Σ_i(q_i⊗m_iq̈_i−m_iq̈_i⊗q_i). Grouping each pair gives (q_i−q_j)⊗F_ij−F_ij⊗(q_i−q_j)=0 because [F2] makes F_ij parallel to q_i−q_j. Thus J̇=0. Applying [F4] to P and to each component of J on every closed subinterval shows both are constant. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, let $\Omega$ and $\mathcal T_h$ be as in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], and let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. The
exact weak problem has a unique solution $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, and the
discrete problem has a unique solution $u_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$. The exact
existence argument uses Countable Choice through Hilbert-space structure and
Lax–Milgram. The finite-dimensional discrete existence and uniqueness
argument uses no choice principle.

1.1 Let $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ with its $H^1$ Hilbert norm. For $v,w\in V$, $|a(v,w)|\le\|
abla v\|_2\|
abla w\|_2\le\|v\|_{H^1}\|w\|_{H^1}.$ By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|
abla v\|_2^2\le(1+C_P^2)\|
abla v\|_2^2$, so $a(v,v)\ge(1+C_P^2)^{-1}\|v\|_{H^1}^2$. Also $|F(v)|\le\|f\|_2\|v\|_2\le C_P\|f\|_2\|v\|_{H^1}$. Thus [F3] gives a unique exact weak solution. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], write the finite-dimensional space in its explicit face basis. The matrix of $a_h$ in this basis is positive definite: for any coefficient vector $c$, its quadratic form is $\|\nabla_h\sum_Fc_F\phi_F\|_2^2$, which vanishes only for the zero coefficient vector by [F5] and basis independence. Hence the matrix is invertible by finite-dimensional linear algebra. The load vector has finite entries because every basis function is piecewise affine and in $L^2$, so Holder [F1] gives $|F_h(\phi_F)|\le\|f\|_2\|\phi_F\|_2$. Solving the finite linear system gives exactly one $u_h$. If there are no interior facets, the space is zero and its unique element $u_h=0$ solves the vacuous equations. This discrete argument is the explicit face-basis matrix solve; [F3] is used only for the exact continuous problem in step 1.1. Thus the discrete proof itself makes no choice. [F1, F4, F5, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$ and let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nondegenerate affine simplex, let $r>1/2$, and let $q\in H^r(K;\mathbb R^d)$ in the restriction convention of [[def-nitsche-restriction-bessel-potential-sobolev-spaces]]. Suppose $\operatorname{div}q\in L^2(K)$ distributionally. Then for every $v\in H^1(K)$,
$$\int_Kq\cdot\nabla v\,dx+\int_K(\operatorname{div}q)v\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(T_Fq\cdot n_{K,F})T_Fv\,dS,$$
where $T_Fq$ is the fractional $L^2(F)$ trace of [[lem-nitsche-fractional-face-trace-on-simplex]], $T_Fv$ is the weak $H^1$ endpoint trace of [[lem-nitsche-scaled-fractional-simplex-trace]] (agreeing with the Fourier trace whenever $v$ has a restriction-space extension), and $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit normal. This identifies the fractional facet trace of $q$ as its weak conormal flux.

Now let $\Omega$ be a nonempty bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$, let $u\in H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ with $r>1/2$, and suppose $-\Delta u=f\in L^2(\Omega)$ distributionally. The traces of $\nabla u$ from the two cells incident to every interior facet agree as vectors, so their outward normal fluxes cancel. For every $w\in H^1(\Omega)$ the sum of the cell identities is
$$\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla w\,dx-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}\int_F\partial_nu\,T_Fw\,dS=\int_\Omega fw\,dx.$$
Here $\mathcal F_h^\partial$ is the set of boundary facets, $\partial_nu:=T_F(\nabla u)\cdot n_F$, and all interior-facet value traces of a global $H^1(\Omega)$ function agree.

## Example

2.1 Let $\phi$ be the P1 hat function at $x=h=1/2$, let $\chi_h\in S_h(0,1)$ have nodal values $(0,0,1)$, and write $u_h=U\phi+\chi_h$. Put $D=\epsilon+\tau b^2$. Since $\phi'=1/h$ on the left cell and $-1/h$ on the right, $\int_0^1(\phi')^2dx=2/h$ and $\int_0^1\phi'\phi\,dx=\frac12[\phi^2]_0^1=0$, so $a_h(\phi,\phi)=2D/h$. Thus $a_h(\chi_h,\phi)=-D/h+b/2$ and the one interior equation is $D(2U-1)/h+b/2=0$. By [F3], $D=\epsilon+(bh/2)(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-1/\mathrm{Pe})=(bh/2)\coth(\mathrm{Pe})$, so $U=(1-\tanh(\mathrm{Pe}))/2=1/(e^{2\mathrm{Pe}}+1)$. The exact value $u(h)=(e^{bh/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{2bh/\epsilon}-1)$ is the same number because $2\mathrm{Pe}=bh/\epsilon$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At $x=0.99$, the piecewise-linear value is $u_h(0.99)=0.98+0.02U$, which tends to $0.98$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The exact value is $(e^{0.99b/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{b/\epsilon}-1)$, which tends to zero because $b>0$ and $0.99<1$. Therefore the pointwise error tends to $0.98$. Consider either the no-flux TPFA cell system of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic grid system of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. Write its finite index set as $I$, its positive diagonal mass matrix as $M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)$, and its stiffness matrix as $L$. In both cases $L=L^{\mathsf T}$, $L\mathbf1=0$, and $L_{ij}=-c_{ij}$ for $i\ne j$, where $c_{ij}=c_{ji}\ge0$. For each species $r$, let $d_r\ge0$ and solve $M u_r'+d_rLu_r=0$. Assume $a_r\le b_r$ for every species. If initially $u_{i,r}\in[a_r,b_r]$ for all $i,r$, then the solution exists for all $t\ge0$ and remains in those intervals. More precisely, each species evolution matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums one, so it is a contraction in the maximum norm. The flow also preserves each weighted species sum $\sum_i m_i u_{i,r}$ and therefore every finite linear combination of species sums, including $\mathcal M_{c,h}$ of [[def-stoichiometric-mass-invariant]].

## Statement

Fix $k,R>0$ and $\ell\ge0$. On $r=R$, write one radial mode as $u(r)=A h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)+B h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)$, where $h_\ell^{(2)}=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}}$. If $u$ satisfies $\partial_ru-iku=0$ at $R$, then
$$B=-\frac{(h_\ell^{(1)})'(kR)-ih_\ell^{(1)}(kR)}{(h_\ell^{(2)})'(kR)-ih_\ell^{(2)}(kR)}A.$$
The denominator is nonzero. For $A\ne0$, the exact reflected modal-amplitude ratio is therefore
$$\frac BA=-\frac{(h_\ell^{(1)})'(kR)-ih_\ell^{(1)}(kR)}{(h_\ell^{(2)})'(kR)-ih_\ell^{(2)}(kR)}.$$
If $A=0$, the coefficient equality forces $B=0$ and no ratio is defined. No uniform-in-$\ell$ smallness is asserted.

For a triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites with affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $T$ the number of triangles, and $E$ the number of edges. Then
$$T=2n-2-k,\qquad E=3n-3-k.$$
In particular $T<2n$ and $E<3n$.

series evaluator correctly returns `domain` at $z=-2$ because this input lies

## Statement

with value $1$ at $z=0$. The right side has a principal analytic
continuation to $\mathbb C\setminus[1,\infty)$, which includes $z=-2$; the
series evaluator correctly returns `domain` at $z=-2$ because this input lies
outside the defined power-series branch. This example distinguishes the

1.1 For $a=b=1,c=2$, the Pochhammer products give $(1)_k=k!$ and $(2)_k=(k+1)!$, so each coefficient is $1/(k+1)$. For $|z|<1$, the geometric series converges uniformly along the segment $sz$ ($0\le s\le1$). Parameterizing the path and integrating the real and imaginary component power series termwise by [F4] gives $$\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{z^{k+1}}{k+1} =\int_0^1\frac{z}{1-sz}\,ds=-\operatorname{Log}(1-z),$$ where [F2], [F3], and [F4] justify the path integral identity since $\operatorname{Re}(1-sz)>0$ along the segment. Dividing by $z$ gives the formula, and the series gives value $1$ at $z=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The principal logarithm is holomorphic when $1-z$ avoids the nonpositive real axis, that is, when $z\notin[1,\infty)$. The quotient has a removable value at $z=0$ by step 1.1, so it defines the stated continuation domain, which contains $-2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

## Example

For $k\ge1$, let $h_k=2^{-k}$ and define the bounded cellwise functions
$$ V_k(x,t)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{\lfloor x/h_k\rfloor},&0\le x<1,\\0,&x\notin[0,1),\end{cases} \qquad 0<t<1. $$
Then $|V_k|\le1$, but $(V_k)$ has no strongly $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-convergent
subsequence. These are a bounded sequence of cell reconstructions illustrating
why a compactness premise is explicit in the weak-limit theorem; they are not
asserted to arise from one fixed initial datum or from a stable update.

## Statement

For the data of [[def-euler-star-pressure-response]], let
$$\Phi(0+):=u_R-u_L-\frac{2(c_L+c_R)}{\gamma-1}.$$
The residual $\Phi$ is $C^1$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
If $\Phi(0+)<0$, then $\Phi$ has exactly one zero $p_*>0$. By the acoustic
wave-response lemma this is the unique positive pressure at which the left and
right wave curves can be joined by a contact. It lies in the
explicit bracket $0<p_*<P$, where, writing
$D=\max\{0,u_L-u_R\}$ and $K=\sqrt{A_L}+\sqrt{A_R}$,
$$P=2\max\{p_L,p_R\}+\frac{6D^2}{K^2}+p_L.$$
If $\Phi(0+)\ge0$, then there is no positive matching pressure. The limiting
left and right rarefaction-tail velocities are ordered with a vacuum gap, or
coincide at the zero-pressure equality threshold. No other vacuum condition is
asserted.

3.1 If $\Phi(0+)<0$, continuity at the extended endpoint $0$ gives some $\epsilon\in(0,P)$ with $\Phi(\epsilon)<0$. ## Statement

Fix $\gamma>1$, $\varepsilon>0$, a finite nonempty node set $J$, positive
weights $w_j$ summing to one, and candidate states $V_j\in\mathbb R^3$ with
mean $\bar V=\sum_jw_jV_j\in K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$. Apply the maximal
convex scaling limiter of
[[alg-pe03-convex-scaling-positivity-limiter]] with $K=K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$.
Its output is well-defined, every limited node lies in $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$,
and the weighted cell mean remains $\bar V$. Hence every limited node has
positive density and positive pressure. If the unscaled nodes already lie in
$K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$, the maximal parameter is $\theta_*=1$. In
particular, if smooth target states stay a distance at least $\delta>0$ from
$\mathbb R^3\setminus K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ and each reconstruction node
has error less than $\delta$, the limiter is inactive and preserves that
reconstruction's accuracy. No positivity between finitely many nodes is
claimed.

1.1 The feasible parameter set $S=\{\theta\in[0,1]:\bar V+\theta(V_j-\bar V)\in K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}\text{ for every }j\}$ contains $0$. Each node map is continuous and $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ is closed by [F3], so each inverse image is closed; the finite intersection $S$ is closed in compact $[0,1]$. Thus $S$ is nonempty compact and has a maximum $\theta_*$. By its definition, every limited node lies in $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 If every original $V_j\in K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$, then $1\in S$, so $\theta_*=1$. If a target state has distance at least $\delta$ from the complement and the candidate differs from it by less than $\delta$, the candidate belongs to $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$; applying this at every node makes $1$ feasible. Thus the limiter leaves all candidates unchanged under the stated strict margin, and their reconstruction error is unchanged. The conclusion concerns only the supplied nodes. [given, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$. If $d=1$, let $\Omega=(a,b)$, $a<b$, have a finite oriented interval mesh $\mathcal T_h$ from [[def-pe04-one-dimensional-interval-mesh-and-broken-polynomials]]; if $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$. Let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and let $u\in C^1([0,T]\times\overline\Omega)$ solve $u_t+\beta\cdot\nabla u=0$ with inflow data equal to its boundary trace. Assume Countable Choice for the imported affine-simplex Green and Lebesgue-measure suppliers; the full-support and finite-measure properties on each cell are established below. Let $u_h$ be the semidiscrete upwind DG solution of degree $p\ge0$, and let $\Pi_h$ be the cellwise L2 projection with respect to Lebesgue measure on each cell. Use $\|w\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\sum_K\int_K|w|^2\,dx$ and put $\eta=\Pi_hu-u$. For an interior face with chosen normal $n_F$, let $\eta^{\mathrm{up}}$ be the trace of $\eta$ from the upwind side. In dimension one, face and boundary integrals are sums with respect to zero-dimensional surface measure. Define
$$R_h(t)^2=\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|\,|\eta^{\mathrm{up}}|^2\,dS+\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)|\eta|^2\,dS.$$
Then
$$\|u_h(T)-u(T)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\left(\|u_h(0)-\Pi_hu(0)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+2\int_0^TR_h(t)^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}+\|\Pi_hu(T)-u(T)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
This is an exact projection-trace residual bound. It asserts no mesh-order rate unless the displayed projection errors are separately estimated.

4.1 Integrate the remaining $-(\beta\theta,\nabla\theta)_K$ by parts using [F3] for $d\ge2$ and [F12] on intervals for $d=1$, then pair cells using [F4] for $d\ge2$ or the endpoint convention in [F7] for $d=1$. At an interior face the homogeneous upwind terms combine to $\frac12\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|[\theta]^2$; at inflow the volume term is $\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|\theta^2$, and at outflow the homogeneous term is $\frac12\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\theta^2$. By the face flux differences from step 3.1, inflow contributes no projection residual because both fluxes use $g$; interior and outflow residuals move to the right with signs $+\int_F(\beta\cdot n_F)\eta^{\mathrm{up}}[\theta]$ and $-\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\eta\theta$, respectively. Hence
$$\frac12\frac d{dt}\|\theta\|_2^2+\frac12\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{int}}}\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|[\theta]^2+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|\theta^2+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\theta^2=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{int}}}\int_F(\beta\cdot n_F)\eta^{\mathrm{up}}[\theta]-\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\eta\theta.$$
[F3, F4, F7, F12, A1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For each interior face use $|b||\eta^{\mathrm{up}}||[\theta]|\le\frac{|b|}{4}[\theta]^2+|b||\eta^{\mathrm{up}}|^2$, and on outflow use $b|\eta||\theta|\le\frac b4\theta^2+b|\eta|^2$. Absorbing the first terms into the half-dissipation terms of step 4.1 and dropping the remaining nonnegative boundary and jump terms gives $\frac d{dt}\|\theta\|_2^2\le2R_h(t)^2$. [step 4.1, algebra]

By the construction in [F11], the projection coefficients solve that fixed finite linear system with moments $\int_Ku(t)\phi_i\,dx$. Since $u_t$ is continuous on the compact space-time cell, [F12] and uniform continuity show that the difference quotients of $u$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $u_t$; the bounded test polynomials and finite measure from step 1.3 therefore allow passage through each moment integral. The coefficients, and hence $\Pi_Ku$, are differentiable in time, so differentiating [F2] gives $(\eta_t,	heta)_K=0$. If $p=0$, then $
abla	heta=0$; if $p\ge1$, then $
abla	heta\in\mathbb P_{p-1}(K)^d$. Since $ eta$ is constant, in either case $ eta\cdot
abla	heta\in\mathbb P_p(K)$ and $(\eta, eta\cdot
abla	heta)_K=0$. This leaves only the transport error and the upwind face-flux differences. [F1, F2, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $K_k$ is injective through $I-K_k$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ there is a unique $u\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ solving $(I-K_k)u=f$, and $A_k:=I-K_k$ has a bounded inverse. Writing $R_k:=\|A_k^{-1}\|$, every $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$\|u-v\|_2\le R_k\|f-(I-K_k)v\|_2.$$
This is an operator-theoretic Fredholm branch; no physical uniqueness statement for the exterior PDE is asserted.

1.1 By [A1], $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is Banach. By [F1] $K_k$ is compact, and the assumed injectivity permits [F2] to be applied to $A_k=I-K_k$. Therefore $A_k$ is surjective and has a bounded inverse; for each $f$ the unique solution is $u=A_k^{-1}f$. [given, A1, F1, F2]

2.1 For arbitrary $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, linearity gives $A_k(u-v)=A_ku-A_kv=f-A_kv$. Applying the bounded inverse from step 1.1 yields $u-v=A_k^{-1}(f-A_kv)$, so $\|u-v\|_2\le\|A_k^{-1}\|\,\|f-A_kv\|_2=R_k\|f-(I-K_k)v\|_2$. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $R>0$, $k>0$, and $Q\in C([0,R];\mathbb C)$. Set $q(x)=Q(|x|)$ on $B_R$ and $q(x)=0$ outside $B_R$. Choose for every $\ell$ an orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell m}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$. Suppose $u^{\rm inc}$ is a classical free Helmholtz field on all of $\mathbb R^3$, and $u=u^{\rm inc}+V$ satisfies the volume-potential equation $V(x)=\int_{B_R}G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)dy$. Assume $u$ is continuous on $\overline B_R$, piecewise $C^2$ on either side of $|x|=R$, and $u$ and its radial derivative are continuous across that interface. For every spherical harmonic $Y_{\ell m}$ assume its coefficient
$$w_{\ell m}(r):=r\int_{S^2}u(r\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega)}d\sigma(\omega)$$
satisfies the regular-origin condition $w_{\ell m}(r)=O(r^{\ell+1})$ as $r\downarrow0$. Explicitly assume the incident regular-mode form: for every $\ell,m$ there is $\alpha_{\ell m}\in\mathbb C$ such that $r\int_{S^2}u^{\rm inc}(r\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega)}d\sigma(\omega)=\alpha_{\ell m}rj_\ell(kr)$ for $r>0$. The outgoing radiation condition is $\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in S^2}|r(\partial_rV(r\omega)-ikV(r\omega))|=0$. Then each reduced mode satisfies
$$w_{\ell m}''(r)+\left(k^2+Q(r)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}\right)w_{\ell m}(r)=0\quad(0<r<R),$$
is regular at $0$, and has for $r>R$ the form
$$w_{\ell m}(r)=\alpha_{\ell m}rj_\ell(kr)+\beta_{\ell m}rh_\ell^{(1)}(kr).$$
The interior and exterior values and first derivatives agree at $R$. This is a conditional mode reduction and matching statement; it asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of the total field.

1.2 The stated origin condition is precisely the regular branch condition for this reduced mode and is retained as a hypothesis, so no singular solution is admitted. Because $u$ and its first derivatives are continuous across $r=R$, integration against the fixed smooth harmonic gives continuity of $w_{\ell m}$ and $w_{\ell m}'$ there. [given, algebra]

1.3 Outside $B_R$, the scattered field $V$ solves the free Helmholtz equation by [F1]. Its angular coefficient $v_{\ell m}(r)=\int_{S^2}V(r\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega)}d\sigma$ solves the free radial equation, whose independent solutions are $j_\ell(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ by the nonzero Wronskian in [F4]; write $v_{\ell m}=a j_\ell(kr)+b h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$. The uniform radiation condition, integrated against the bounded $Y_{\ell m}$, gives $r(v'_{\ell m}-ikv_{\ell m})\to0$. Put $\vartheta=kr-\ell\pi/2$ and $c=(-i)^{\ell+1}$. ## Statement

Assume the homogeneous one-dimensional problem and uniform P1 SUPG form of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]] and [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]]. Assume Countable Choice, and let $u\in C^2([0,1])$ be the exact solution and $u_h\in V_h$ the unique discrete solution from [[thm-supg-one-dimensional-consistency-coercivity]]. For every continuous, piecewise-H1 function $w$ with $w(0)=w(1)=0$, define
$$\|w\|_{\mathrm{SD}}^2:=\epsilon\|w'\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2+\tau b^2\|w'\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2,\qquad M:=\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$
This is the product $L^2$ norm of $(\sqrt{\epsilon}w',\sqrt{\tau}|b|w')$, so it has the triangle inequality.
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le \left[h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}+h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}+\frac{h^2}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right]M.$$
With $c_*$ from [[lem-supg-one-dimensional-optimal-parameter]], there is a universal $C_*>0$ such that also
$$\|u-u_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le C_*\left(h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|}\right)M.$$

5.1 From [F5], $h|b|\sqrt{\tau}\le h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|/2}$. Finally $h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}\le h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}$. These inequalities prove the second estimate with a universal constant depending only on $c_*$. [F1, F5, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under the finite-dimensional hypotheses of [[alg-phase-field-sav-cahn-hilliard-step]], the displayed SAV linear system has a unique solution at every step. Every solution conserves the discrete mean and obeys
$$\widetilde E_h(u^{n+1},r^{n+1})+\frac\kappa2\langle A_h\delta u,\delta u\rangle_h+(\delta r)^2+M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h=\widetilde E_h(u^n,r^n),$$
where $\delta u=u^{n+1}-u^n$, $\delta r=r^{n+1}-r^n$, and
$$\widetilde E_h(u,r)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+r^2.$$
Thus $\widetilde E_h$ is nonincreasing. This conclusion is about the modified energy; it does not assert monotonicity of the original physical energy $\mathcal E_h(u)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+E_{1,h}(u)$.

## Statement

For $n\ge1$ and $0\le d<n$, define
$$\lambda_i(x)=\frac{(-1)^i}{\prod_{k=i}^{i+d}(x-x_k)},\qquad \mu_i(x)=\prod_{j<i}(x-x_j)\prod_{k>i+d}(x_k-x), \qquad 0\le i\le n-d,$$
where empty products equal $1$. Put $s(x)=\sum_i\mu_i(x)$ and let $p_i$ be
the window polynomials in [[def-floater-hormann-window-polynomial]]. For
$x\notin\{x_0,\ldots,x_n\}$, the Floater–Hormann quotient is
$$r_d(x)=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i(x)p_i(x)}{\sum_i\lambda_i(x)} =\frac{\sum_i\mu_i(x)p_i(x)}{s(x)}.$$
Moreover, clearing the node factors in the barycentric denominator gives
$\prod_{j=0}^n(x-x_j)\sum_i\lambda_i(x)=(-1)^{n-d}s(x)$.
After clearing and canceling the displayed factors, this is a polynomial
identity valid at every real $x$, including the nodes.
Expanding this expression into a support-node barycentric quotient gives
exactly the weights in [[def-floater-hormann-interpolant]]. Its continuous
values at the nodes are the assigned data.

1.1 Put $P_0(x)=\prod_{j=0}^n(x-x_j)$ and $m=n-d$. Counting the $m$ factors to the right of a window gives $$\mu_i(x)=(-1)^mP_0(x)\lambda_i(x).$$ Indeed, after cancellation each right factor $x_k-x$ contributes one minus sign when rewritten as $x-x_k$, and the remaining denominator factors are exactly the window nodes. Thus the cleared products agree as polynomials, including at nodes; summing gives the stated cleared-denominator identity. Away from nodes it also shows that the blend quotient with $\lambda_i$ equals the quotient with $\mu_i$ and $s$. [given, construct, algebra]

3.1 At a node $x_\alpha$, $\mu_i(x_\alpha)$ is zero unless $\max(0,\alpha-d)\le i\le\min(\alpha,m)$; for these indices all its factors are positive. This index set is nonempty, and every corresponding window contains $x_\alpha$. By [F2], $p_i(x_\alpha)=f_\alpha$, so the blend has numerator $f_\alpha s(x_\alpha)$ and $s(x_\alpha)>0$. Its value is therefore $f_\alpha$, agreeing with the support convention in [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take two spin-$1/2$ sites with computational basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, Pauli matrix $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, and finite Hamiltonian
$$H=-Z\otimes I-I\otimes Z-Z\otimes Z.$$
Supply the initial product state $|11\rangle$ by the rank-one open-boundary TT cores $G_k(1,i_k,1)=1_{\{i_k=2\}}$ for $k=1,2$. Starting from this presentation, one completed width-two exact sweep of [[alg-na-alternating-tensor-optimization-and-effective-eigenproblems]] returns $|00\rangle$ and lowers the energy from $1$ to $-3$.

1.1 In the displayed basis, $H$ is the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-3,1,1,1)$: the three summands contribute respectively $(-1,-1,1,1)$, $(-1,1,-1,1)$, and $(-1,1,1,-1)$. Thus $|00\rangle$ is the unique unit ground vector with energy $-3$, while $|11\rangle$ has energy $1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For the only two-site window, the fixed environments are identities, so the embedding $E$ and effective Hamiltonian are $I_4$ and $H$. The exact solve in [F2] therefore selects $|00\rangle$. The backward pass sees the same $H$ and leaves this unique ground vector unchanged, and its exact SVD split has rank one and no discarded tail. Hence the completed sweep returns $|00\rangle$ with energy $-3<1$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $E$ be a side of a shape-regular polygon of diameter $H$ with a matching quasiuniform $P_1$ boundary mesh of size $h$. Let $\theta_E$ be the piecewise-linear boundary function equal to $1$ at the interior nodes of $E$ and $0$ at the endpoints and all other boundary nodes. For

$$\|q\|_{00,E}^2:=\int_E\int_E\frac{|q(s)-q(t)|^2}{|s-t|^2}\,ds\,dt+\int_E\frac{|q(s)|^2}{\operatorname{dist}(s,\partial E)}\,ds,$$

one has $\|\theta_E\|_{00,E}^2\le C(1+\log(H/h))$. Also every continuous piecewise-affine $u_h$ on $\Omega_i$ satisfies

$$\|u_h-\overline u_{\Omega_i}\|_{L^\infty(\Omega_i)}^2\le C(1+\log(H_i/h_i))\|\nabla u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega_i)}^2.$$

Consequently, for the edge mean $\overline u_E$,

$$\|I_h(\theta_E(u_h-\overline u_E))\|_{00,E}^2\le C(1+\log(H_i/h_i))^2\|\nabla u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega_i)}^2,$$

where $I_h$ is nodal piecewise-linear interpolation on $E$.

1.1 If $E$ has no interior boundary node, then $\theta_E=0$. If $|E|/h\le4$, scaling $E$ to unit length gives a uniform bound on both terms of $\|\theta_E\|_{00,E}^2$. Otherwise the first and last mesh intervals have length comparable to $h$, $\theta_E$ is linear from $0$ to $1$ and from $1$ to $0$ there, and it equals $1$ between them. The weighted integral on either endpoint interval is bounded by $\int_0^h(s/h)^2\,ds/s\le C$; the plateau contributes at most $C+\log(|E|/h)\le C+\log(H/h)$. In the double integral, pairs in the plateau contribute zero. Pairs within one endpoint interval have integrand at most $Ch^{-2}$ and hence contribute at most a constant. For one point $s$ in an endpoint interval and one outside it, integrating $(1-s/h)^2/(t-s)^2$ in the outside variable and then in $s$ gives a constant; the two endpoint intervals are treated in the same way. Therefore $\|\theta_E\|_{00,E}^2\le C(1+\log(H/h))$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Put $v_h=u_h-\overline u_{\Omega_i}$ and $M=\|v_h\|_{L^\infty(\Omega_i)}$. Since $v_h$ is affine on each triangle, $M$ is attained at a mesh vertex $x_0$. The uniform interior-cone parameter in [F1] supplies constants $c_0,\omega_0>0$, independent of $i$ and $h_i$, such that from every such vertex there is an inward cone of height at least $c_0H_i$ and opening at least $\omega_0$ contained in $\Omega_i$. Use the annulus in this cone with radii between $c_0H_i/2$ and $c_0H_i$. Shape regularity and quasiuniformity give a bounded vertex patch $\omega_{x_0}$ and $$\|
abla v_h\|_{L^\infty(\omega_{x_0})}\le Ch_i^{-1}\|
abla v_h\|_{L^2(\omega_{x_0})}.$$ Thus the difference from $x_0$ to distance $ch_i$ on any cone ray is at most $C\|
abla v_h\|_{L^2(\omega_{x_0})}$. For $r\ge ch_i$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$\left|\int_{ch_i}^r\partial_s v_h(x_0+s e_	heta)\,dsight|^2\le \log\!\left( rac{r}{ch_i}ight)\int_{ch_i}^r|
abla v_h(x_0+s e_	heta)|^2s\,ds.$$ At each point in the annulus, express $v_h(x_0)$ as its value there plus these two path differences, square using $|a+b+c|^2\le3(|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2)$, and integrate in polar coordinates over the annulus. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1/2<r\le1$, and let $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap
H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ solve $-\Delta u=f\in L^2(\Omega)$ on a bounded connected
Lipschitz polyhedral domain. On any finite matching shape-regular mesh, the
solution $u_h$ of the Crouzeix–Raviart method satisfies
$$\|u-u_h\|_{\sharp,h}\le C h^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}.$$
In particular, $\|\nabla_h(u-u_h)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ obeys the same bound.
The constant is independent of the mesh size and may depend on $\Omega$, $d$,
the shape-regularity bound, and $r$.

2.1 On an interior facet, $[u-I_h^{CR}u]=-[I_h^{CR}u]$ because $u$ has a common trace; on a boundary facet its trace is $-I_h^{CR}u$ because $u$ has zero trace. The face terms in [F3], squared and summed over facets with each cell incident to at most $d+1$ facets, give $\sum_F h_F^{-1}\|[u-I_h^{CR}u]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2 \le Ch^{2r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}^2.$ Together with step 1.1, this proves $\|u-I_h^{CR}u\|_{\sharp,h}\le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}$, hence the same upper bound for the infimum in [F6]. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F6] using steps 2.1, 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4. The constants $M_h=1$ and $\alpha_h=(1+C_J)^{-1}$ are uniform, so its estimate gives $\|u-u_h\|_{\sharp,h}\le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}$. The interpolation and consistency constants depend only on $d$, shape regularity, and $r$, and the jump constant $C_J$ has the same dependence. ## Statement

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, grid width $h$, particle count $P\ge1$, and final time $T>0$. Apply classical RK4 from [[alg-periodic-pic-classical-rk4-step]] to the autonomous finite-dimensional PIC system
$$ \dot Z=F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z),\qquad (F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z))_p=\frac1P\sum_{r=1}^P \mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(z_p,z_r),\qquad z_p=(X_p,V_p). $$ Let $Z(t)$ be an exact solution on $[0,T]$. Assume $F_{\varepsilon,h}$ is $C^4$ on an open set containing a common compact convex tube $\mathcal T$; the exact path, all numerical states, and every RK4 stage generated from both the exact and numerical starting states lie in $\mathcal T$; and all derivatives of $F_{\varepsilon,h}$ through order four are bounded there. Choose a uniform step $0<h_t\le h_0$ with $h_0>0$, initialize exactly, and retain every time $t_k=kh_t\le T$ for integers $k\ge0$; $T/h_t$ need not be an integer. The stage hypotheses concern each step ending by $T$. Put $$ L_F=2L_{\varepsilon,h},\qquad L_*=L_Fe^{L_Fh_0}, $$ and choose $C_4$ so that the exact-start defect on this tube is at most $C_4s^5$ for admitted steps $0<s\le h_0$ ending by $T$. The local-order supplier gives such constants for a sufficiently small positive $h_0$ under the stated smoothness and tube assumptions. Then, for every grid time $t_k=kh_t\le T$, $$ \|Z_k-Z(t_k)\|_2\le \begin{cases} C_4\dfrac{e^{L_*T}-1}{L_*}h_t^4,&L_*>0,\\[4pt] C_4Th_t^4,&L_*=0. \end{cases} $$
The tube, exact-solution, and stage-admissibility hypotheses are conditional; this is a fixed-$\varepsilon$, fixed-grid finite-particle time error, not a continuum or singular-force estimate.

2.1 Let $E_k=\|Z_k-Z(t_k)\|_2$. The RK4 stages from the paired exact and numerical starts are admitted by assumption, so [F3] bounds the difference of their one-step outputs by $(1+L_*h_t)E_k$. Adding the exact-start defect from step 1.1 by the triangle inequality gives $E_{k+1}\le(1+L_*h_t)E_k+C_4h_t^5$, with $E_0=0$. [F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Unroll step 2.1 over the first $k$ steps to get $E_k\le C_4h_t^5\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1+L_*h_t)^j$, including the empty sum at $k=0$. If $L_*>0$, the finite geometric sum gives $E_k\le C_4h_t^4[(1+L_*h_t)^k-1]/L_*$. Since $1+u\le e^u$ for $u\ge0$ and $kh_t=t_k\le T$, this is at most $C_4h_t^4(e^{L_*T}-1)/L_*$. If $L_*=0$, the sum gives $E_k\le C_4kh_t^5=C_4t_kh_t^4\le C_4Th_t^4$. These are the claimed bounds on every retained partial-grid time, without requiring a step at $T$. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, grid width $h$, particle count $P\ge1$, and final time $T>0$. Apply classical RK4 from [[alg-periodic-pic-classical-rk4-step]] to the autonomous finite-dimensional PIC system
$$ \dot Z=F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z),\qquad (F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z))_p=\frac1P\sum_{r=1}^P \mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(z_p,z_r),\qquad z_p=(X_p,V_p). $$ Let $Z(t)$ be an exact solution on $[0,T]$. Assume $F_{\varepsilon,h}$ is $C^4$ on an open set containing a common compact convex tube $\mathcal T$; the exact path, all numerical states, and every RK4 stage generated from both the exact and numerical starting states lie in $\mathcal T$; and all derivatives of $F_{\varepsilon,h}$ through order four are bounded there. Choose a uniform step $0<h_t\le h_0$ with $h_0>0$, initialize exactly, and retain every time $t_k=kh_t\le T$ for integers $k\ge0$; $T/h_t$ need not be an integer. The stage hypotheses concern each step ending by $T$. Put $$ L_F=2L_{\varepsilon,h},\qquad L_*=L_Fe^{L_Fh_0}, $$ and choose $C_4$ so that the exact-start defect on this tube is at most $C_4s^5$ for admitted steps $0<s\le h_0$ ending by $T$. The local-order supplier gives such constants for a sufficiently small positive $h_0$ under the stated smoothness and tube assumptions. Then, for every grid time $t_k=kh_t\le T$, $$ \|Z_k-Z(t_k)\|_2\le \begin{cases} C_4\dfrac{e^{L_*T}-1}{L_*}h_t^4,&L_*>0,\\[4pt] C_4Th_t^4,&L_*=0. \end{cases} $$
The tube, exact-solution, and stage-admissibility hypotheses are conditional; this is a fixed-$\varepsilon$, fixed-grid finite-particle time error, not a continuum or singular-force estimate.

1.1 The state field is a mean over $P$ pair interactions. For two stacked states $Z,\widetilde Z$, [F1] gives $|(F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z))_p-(F_{\varepsilon,h}(\widetilde Z))_p| \le L_{\varepsilon,h}|z_p-\widetilde z_p| +\frac{L_{\varepsilon,h}}P\sum_r|z_r-\widetilde z_r|.$ Taking the stacked Euclidean norm and applying finite Cauchy–Schwarz to the average term shows $\|F_{\varepsilon,h}(Z)-F_{\varepsilon,h}(\widetilde Z)\|_2\le2L_{\varepsilon,h}\|Z-\widetilde Z\|_2=L_F\|Z-\widetilde Z\|_2$. The $C^4$ tube hypotheses therefore permit [F2], which gives a uniform exact-start local defect at most $C_4h_t^5$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $E_k=\|Z_k-Z(t_k)\|_2$. The RK4 stages from the paired exact and numerical starts are admitted by assumption, so [F3] bounds the difference of their one-step outputs by $(1+L_*h_t)E_k$. Adding the exact-start defect from step 1.1 by the triangle inequality gives $E_{k+1}\le(1+L_*h_t)E_k+C_4h_t^5$, with $E_0=0$. [F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

1.1 By [F2], the sample pullback and its reciprocal are measurable on $[0,1]$. Over $0\le t\le3/2$, the reciprocal coefficient equals $1$ for lengths $1/2$, $1/2$, and $1/2$ on the successive intervals $[0,1/2)$, $[1/2,1)$, and $[1,3/2)$, except that its value on the middle interval is $1/2$. Thus its integral is $1/2+1/4+1/2=5/4$; dividing by $r=3/2$ gives $\int_0^1a(3y/2)^{-1}dy=5/6$, so $A_r=6/5$. The full-period reciprocal mean is $(1+1/2)/2=3/4$, hence $A^*=4/3$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Therefore $|A_r-A^*|=|6/5-4/3|=2/15$. Here $\lambda=1$, $\Lambda=2$, and $1/r=2/3$, so the bound in [F1] is $2\cdot4\cdot(2/3)=16/3$; indeed $2/15\le16/3$. The example verifies both nonzero resonance and the stated conservative estimate. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Set $K=C^TM_bC$. If the retained electric cochain space is zero-dimensional,
define $\lambda_{\max}:=0$; otherwise set
$$\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{e\ne0}\frac{e^TKe}{e^TM_ee}.$$
For a lossless, source-free update from [[alg-maxwell-yee-leapfrog-update]], define
$$\mathcal E^n:=\frac12(e^n)^TM_ee^n+\frac12(b^{n-1/2})^TM_bb^{n+1/2},\qquad b_c^n:=\frac{b^{n-1/2}+b^{n+1/2}}2.$$
Then $\mathcal E^n$ is independent of $n$, and
$$\mathcal E^n\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}}4\right)\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2.$$
Consequently, the actual strict spectral condition $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$ makes this modified energy positive on admissible staggered states and controls the electric field and the centered magnetic field. When $\lambda_{\max}>0$, at equality the energy loses coercivity and a maximal mode has a repeated root $-1$; above equality a mode grows exponentially. If $\lambda_{\max}=0$, the strict condition is automatic for every $\Delta t>0$ and neither endpoint case occurs.

1.1 If $N_e=0$, the electric cochain is necessarily zero and $C$ is the zero map from the zero space. The Faraday row in [F2] makes $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$ at every step, while the electric row is an equality in the zero space. Thus $b_c^n=b^{n+1/2}$ is constant and $\mathcal E^n=\tfrac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2$. With the stated convention $\lambda_{\max}=0$, this proves conservation, the lower bound, and positivity on the remaining magnetic state for every $\Delta t>0$; there is no positive-eigenvalue endpoint case. For the rest of the proof assume $N_e>0$. The quotient defining $\lambda_{\max}$ is continuous on the compact set $\{e:e^TM_ee=1\}$, so the maximum exists and is finite. Also $e^TKe=(Ce)^TM_b(Ce)\ge0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}\ge0$. From the first row of [F2], $b^{n-1/2}=b_c^n+\Delta t Ce^n/2$ and $b^{n+1/2}=b_c^n-\Delta t Ce^n/2$. Expanding their $M_b$ inner product gives $\mathcal E^n=\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2.$ [F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 Subtract the electric row in [F2] at indices $n$ and $n-1$, then use the magnetic row to replace $b^{n+1/2}-b^{n-1/2}$; this gives $M_e(e^{n+1}-2e^n+e^{n-1})+\Delta t^2Ke^n=0$. If $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}=4$, a maximizing vector $v$ satisfies $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$ by the constrained Rayleigh-quotient maximum. Thus $e^n=q_nv$ obeys $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}q_n=0$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(r+1)^2$. Hence $q_n=(-1)^n(a+bn)$ is a solution and grows linearly when $b\ne0$. It is compatible with the full first-order rows by setting $b^{n+1/2}=(q_{n+1}-q_n)Cv/(\Delta t\lambda_{\max})$: the Ampere row follows from $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$, and the Faraday row follows from the scalar recurrence. For $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}>4$, the same recurrence has real reciprocal roots, one with modulus greater than one. This proves the endpoint caveat and instability above it. [F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Set $K=C^TM_bC$. If the retained electric cochain space is zero-dimensional,
define $\lambda_{\max}:=0$; otherwise set
$$\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{e\ne0}\frac{e^TKe}{e^TM_ee}.$$
For a lossless, source-free update from [[alg-maxwell-yee-leapfrog-update]], define
$$\mathcal E^n:=\frac12(e^n)^TM_ee^n+\frac12(b^{n-1/2})^TM_bb^{n+1/2},\qquad b_c^n:=\frac{b^{n-1/2}+b^{n+1/2}}2.$$
Then $\mathcal E^n$ is independent of $n$, and
$$\mathcal E^n\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}}4\right)\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2.$$
Consequently, the actual strict spectral condition $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$ makes this modified energy positive on admissible staggered states and controls the electric field and the centered magnetic field. When $\lambda_{\max}>0$, at equality the energy loses coercivity and a maximal mode has a repeated root $-1$; above equality a mode grows exponentially. If $\lambda_{\max}=0$, the strict condition is automatic for every $\Delta t>0$ and neither endpoint case occurs.

1.1 If $N_e=0$, the electric cochain is necessarily zero and $C$ is the zero map from the zero space. The Faraday row in [F2] makes $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$ at every step, while the electric row is an equality in the zero space. Thus $b_c^n=b^{n+1/2}$ is constant and $\mathcal E^n=\tfrac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2$. With the stated convention $\lambda_{\max}=0$, this proves conservation, the lower bound, and positivity on the remaining magnetic state for every $\Delta t>0$; there is no positive-eigenvalue endpoint case. For the rest of the proof assume $N_e>0$. The quotient defining $\lambda_{\max}$ is continuous on the compact set $\{e:e^TM_ee=1\}$, so the maximum exists and is finite. Also $e^TKe=(Ce)^TM_b(Ce)\ge0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}\ge0$. From the first row of [F2], $b^{n-1/2}=b_c^n+\Delta t Ce^n/2$ and $b^{n+1/2}=b_c^n-\Delta t Ce^n/2$. 2.1 By the definition of $\lambda_{\max}$, $\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2=(e^n)^TKe^n\le\lambda_{\max}\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2$. Substitution into step 1.1 gives the stated lower bound. ## Example

For the uniform $N$-interval P1 discretization of the Dirichlet Poisson problem
on $(0,1)$, one-level exact point-patch additive Schwarz has
$$ \kappa_A(BA)=\frac{1+\cos(\pi/N)}{1-\cos(\pi/N)}. $$
The patches are the supports of the interior nodal hats; they overlap with
their neighbors and have bounded multiplicity. Nevertheless the condition
number diverges with the number $N-1$ of local spaces.

1.1 Direct expansion gives $x^{\mathsf T}A_Nx=h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(x_j-x_{j-1})^2$ with $x_0=x_N=0$. It is positive for every nonzero vector because vanishing of all successive differences and $x_0=0$ forces every $x_j=0$. For the point-patch injection $R_i=e_i$, the local matrix is $A_i=e_i^{\mathsf T}A_Ne_i=2/h$. Thus [F1] gives $B_N=\sum_i e_i(h/2)e_i^{\mathsf T}=(h/2)I$. Each corresponding nodal hat is supported on two adjacent mesh intervals, so neighboring local supports overlap and at most three closed supports meet at a point. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, set $v_j^{(k)}=\sin(jk\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The endpoints vanish. With $\theta=k\pi/N$, the identity $v_{j-1}^{(k)}+v_{j+1}^{(k)}=2\cos(\theta)v_j^{(k)}$ gives $A_Nv^{(k)}=\frac{2}{h}(1-\cos\theta)v^{(k)}.$ These eigenvalues are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $(0,\pi)$. Since $A_N$ is symmetric, eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal: for $k\ne l$, $(\lambda_k-\lambda_l)(v^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}v^{(l)}=(A_Nv^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}v^{(l)}-(v^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}A_Nv^{(l)}=0$. The vectors are nonzero, so the $N-1$ orthogonal vectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^{N-1}$. Multiplication by $B_N=(h/2)I$ gives eigenvalues $1-\cos(k\pi/N)$ for $B_NA_N$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

Let $f\in\widehat W'$ and set $\widetilde f=E_0^T f$. The constrained minimization problem

$$\min_{w\in\widetilde W,\ Bw=0}\left(\tfrac12\langle\widetilde S w,w\rangle-\langle\widetilde f,w\rangle\right)$$

has the saddle equations $\widetilde S w+B^T\lambda=\widetilde f$, $Bw=0$. Eliminating $w$ gives the FETI-DP dual system

$$B\widetilde S^{-1}B^T\lambda=B\widetilde S^{-1}E_0^Tf.$$

On $\Lambda=\operatorname{range}B$ its matrix is positive definite, and the exact multiplier solution reconstructs the unique assembled interface solution $w\in\widehat W$.

1.1 The Lagrangian is $L(w,\lambda)=\tfrac12\langle\widetilde S w,w\rangle-\langle E_0^Tf,w\rangle+\langle\lambda,Bw\rangle$. Its derivative in arbitrary $z\in\widetilde W$ is $\langle\widetilde S w+B^T\lambda-E_0^Tf,z\rangle$, and its multiplier derivative is $Bw$. Setting both derivatives to zero gives the displayed saddle equations. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
2.1 By [F3], the first equation has the unique solution $w=\widetilde S^{-1}(E_0^Tf-B^T\lambda)$. Substitution into $Bw=0$ gives the displayed dual system. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, grid width $h$, particle count $P\ge1$, and $T>0$. Use uniform RK4 times $t_n=n\Delta t$ for integers $n\ge0$, with $0<\Delta t\le h_0$, where $h_0$ is the positive admitted step-width bound in the RK4 tube/defect hypotheses below. Retain all $t_n\le T$; no integer value of $T/\Delta t$ is required. Assume the smooth fixed-regularization hypotheses of [[thm-periodic-pic-smooth-density-grid-force-consistency]], and that the translated unit-source regularized densities $\eta_\varepsilon(\cdot-y)-L^{-d}$ satisfy its derivative bounds uniformly in $y$. Let $\delta_{\varepsilon,h}$ be the uniform phase-kernel defect from [[thm-periodic-pic-mean-field-error-with-force-defect]]. The consistency theorem gives the explicit estimate
$$ \delta_{\varepsilon,h} \le |cQ|\left[ L^{d/2}h^{2-d/2}\bigl(\gamma_{N,L}C_{\rm src}^{(1)}+C_3^{(1)}\bigr) +C_{\rm int}^{(1)}h^2 \right], $$ where $C_{\rm src}^{(1)},C_3^{(1)},C_{\rm int}^{(1)}$ are the constants of that theorem evaluated at a unit point source; translation of the continuum source leaves their derivative suprema unchanged, while the shape quadrature constants are independent of the translate. Define the RK4 empirical measure by $\nu_{P,h}^{\Delta t}(t_n)=P^{-1}\sum_{p=1}^P\delta_{z_p^{\Delta t}(t_n)}$. Put $$ \delta_0=W_1(\nu_0^h,\mu_0),\qquad C_{\rm RK}= \begin{cases} C_4(e^{L_*T}-1)/L_*,&L_*>0,\\ C_4T,&L_*=0, \end{cases} $$ using the constants of [[thm-periodic-pic-rk4-finite-time-error-on-a-controlled-tube]]. For exact initialization, a common admissible initial coupling, and the same compact-tube hypotheses, the RK4 empirical measure $\nu_{P,h}^{\Delta t}(t_n)$ and regularized characteristic solution $\mu_\varepsilon(t_n)$ satisfy $$ W_1\!\left(\nu_{P,h}^{\Delta t}(t_n),\mu_\varepsilon(t_n)\right) \le \frac{C_{\rm RK}}{\sqrt P}\Delta t^4 +e^{2L_\varepsilon T}\left(\delta_0+T\delta_{\varepsilon,h}\right), \qquad t_n\le T. $$
The terms are time error, prescribed initial empirical error, and fixed-$\varepsilon$ mesh-force error. No universal rate for $\delta_0$ and no $\varepsilon\to0$ singular Vlasov–Poisson limit is asserted.

1.2 Work at a retained time $t=t_n=n\Delta t\le T$ on the stated grid, whose step obeys $0<\Delta t\le h_0$. Let $A$ be the finite support of $
u_0^h$ and $I_a=\{p:z_p^h(0)=a\}$, $m_a=|I_a|$ for $a\in A$. For any prescribed coupling $\pi_0$ of $
u_0^h$ and $\mu_0$, define a measure on the second coordinate for each label $p\in I_a$ by $\lambda_p(B)=\pi_0(\{a\}	imes B)/m_a$. Since $
u_0^h(\{a\})=m_a/P$, each $\lambda_p$ has mass $1/P$, and for each $a$ the sum over $p\in I_a$ is $\pi_0(\{a\}	imes\cdot)$. By the duplicate-path argument in [[thm-periodic-pic-mean-field-error-with-force-defect]], all labels in $I_a$ share the same exact path $X_t(a)$. Thus summing these label measures gives exactly the pushforward $\Pi_t=(X_t,Y_t)_\#\pi_0$, the Dobrushin-transported coupling, where $Y_t$ is the continuum characteristic flow. In particular, $\Pi_t$ has the exact grid and continuum marginals. Its cost is at most $e^{2L_\varepsilon T}(D_0+T\delta_{\varepsilon,h})$ by [F2]. Replace $z_p^h(t)$ in each summand by the RK4 state $z_p^{\Delta t}(t)$. The resulting measure is a coupling of $
u_{P,h}^{\Delta t}(t)$ and $\mu_\varepsilon(t)$, and pointwise triangle inequality increases its cost by at most $P^{-1}\sum_p|z_p^{\Delta t}-z_p^h|$. By Cauchy–Schwarz this is at most $P^{-1/2}\|Z^{\Delta t}-Z^h\|_2\le P^{-1/2}C_{m RK}\Delta t^4$ using [F3]. This gives the claimed bound with $D_0$ in place of $\delta_0$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The bound of step 1.2 holds for every prescribed initial coupling. Taking the infimum of $D_0$ gives $\delta_0$ by [F4], without selecting a minimizing plan. This proves the stated staged error budget. [F4, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

For a fixed macro sample $K$ in [[alg-fehmm-periodic-cell-micro-macro]], let $b_K$ be its sampled coefficient, $w_{K,p}\in V_\#$ the full periodic cell solution, and $w^h_{K,p}\in W_{\mathcal M}$ its micro P1 solution from [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Set $\|\nabla v\|_{b_K}^2=\int_Yb_K|\nabla v|^2$. Then
$$p\cdot(A_K^h-A_K^{\rm ex})p=\|\nabla(w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}^2\ge0,$$
and for any $z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}$,
$$\|\nabla(w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}\le\|\nabla(z_h-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}.$$
In particular $\|A_K^h-A_K^{\rm ex}\|_{op}\le\eta_K^2$, where $\eta_K=\sup_{|p|=1}\inf_{z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}}\|\nabla(z_h-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}$ and $\|M\|_{op}=\sup_{|p|=1}|Mp|$.

1.1 Write $e_p=w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p}$. Subtracting the two variational equations gives $\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla z_h=0$ for every $z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}$. Thus $e_p$ is orthogonal in the $b_K$ gradient inner product to the whole micro space. For any $z_h$, $\|
abla(w_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2=\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}^2+\|
abla(w^h_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2,$ which proves the best-approximation inequality. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $p,q\in\mathbb R^2$, the symmetric energy representation in [F2] and the full/discrete equations imply $p\cdot(A_K^h-A_K^{m ex})q=\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla e_q.$ Indeed, expanding the two energy bilinear forms leaves this term; each cross term vanishes by testing the full equation with the difference in $V_\#$ or the discrete equation with a micro function in $W_{\mathcal M}$. Taking $q=p$ proves the identity. For unit $p,q$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the right side by $\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}\|
abla e_q\|_{b_K}\le\eta_K^2$ by step 1.1. The supremum over unit vectors is the operator norm, giving the final bound. [F2, step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a fixed macro sample $K$ in [[alg-fehmm-periodic-cell-micro-macro]], let $b_K$ be its sampled coefficient, $w_{K,p}\in V_\#$ the full periodic cell solution, and $w^h_{K,p}\in W_{\mathcal M}$ its micro P1 solution from [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Set $\|\nabla v\|_{b_K}^2=\int_Yb_K|\nabla v|^2$. Then
$$p\cdot(A_K^h-A_K^{\rm ex})p=\|\nabla(w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}^2\ge0,$$
and for any $z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}$,
$$\|\nabla(w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}\le\|\nabla(z_h-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}.$$
In particular $\|A_K^h-A_K^{\rm ex}\|_{op}\le\eta_K^2$, where $\eta_K=\sup_{|p|=1}\inf_{z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}}\|\nabla(z_h-w_{K,p})\|_{b_K}$ and $\|M\|_{op}=\sup_{|p|=1}|Mp|$.

1.1 Write $e_p=w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p}$. Subtracting the two variational equations gives $\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla z_h=0$ for every $z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}$. Thus $e_p$ is orthogonal in the $b_K$ gradient inner product to the whole micro space. For any $z_h$, $\|
abla(w_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2=\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}^2+\|
abla(w^h_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2,$ which proves the best-approximation inequality. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $p,q\in\mathbb R^2$, the symmetric energy representation in [F2] and the full/discrete equations imply $p\cdot(A_K^h-A_K^{m ex})q=\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla e_q.$ Indeed, expanding the two energy bilinear forms leaves this term; each cross term vanishes by testing the full equation with the difference in $V_\#$ or the discrete equation with a micro function in $W_{\mathcal M}$. Taking $q=p$ proves the identity. For unit $p,q$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the right side by $\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}\|
abla e_q\|_{b_K}\le\eta_K^2$ by step 1.1. The supremum over unit vectors is the operator norm, giving the final bound. [F2, step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take two unit cells on $(0,2)$, one interior face with transmissibility $T=1$, no-flux boundary faces, $\varepsilon=\kappa=M=\tau=1$, and $u^0=(1,-1)$. The discrete mean is zero, and the one-step convex-splitting state is $u^1=(a,-a)$ where $a$ is the unique root in $(0,1)$ of $2a^3+7a-5=0$. The initial energy is $2$ and the new energy is $2a^2+\frac12(1-a^2)^2<2$.

## Example

Take two unit cells on $(0,2)$, one interior face with transmissibility $T=1$, no-flux boundary faces, $\varepsilon=\kappa=M=\tau=1$, and $u^0=(1,-1)$. The discrete mean is zero, and the one-step convex-splitting state is $u^1=(a,-a)$ where $a$ is the unique root in $(0,1)$ of $2a^3+7a-5=0$. The initial energy is $2$ and the new energy is $2a^2+\frac12(1-a^2)^2<2$.

1.1 The initial mean is zero, so mass conservation [F2] forces $u^1=(a,-a)$. Since $A_h(a,-a)=(2a,-2a)$ and $F_c'(s)=s^3+s$, $F_e'(s)=2s$, the first chemical-potential component is $\mu_1=2a+(a^3+a)-2=a^3+3a-2$. The first state equation gives $a-1=-2\mu_1$, hence $2a^3+7a-5=0$. The polynomial is strictly increasing because its derivative is $6a^2+7>0$, and its values at $0$ and $1$ are $-5$ and $4$; therefore it has exactly one root $a\in(0,1)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The initial gradient energy is $\frac12\langle A_hu^0,u^0\rangle_h=2$ and both potential terms vanish, so $E_h(u^0)=2$. For $u^1=(a,-a)$ the gradient energy is $2a^2$ and the potential energy is $\frac12(1-a^2)^2$. Since $0<a<1$, $(1-a^2)^2<1-a^2$, hence $E_h(u^1)<2=E_h(u^0)$. This is the exact finite ledger for the step. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty, bounded, and open. Write $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, $B=\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)$, and let $P_B$ denote the $H$-orthogonal projection onto $B$. Let $S_h\subset H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $V_h\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ be finite-dimensional subspaces with $B_h=\nabla S_h\subset V_h$. Suppose linear projections $\Pi_h^0:H_0^1\to S_h$ and $\Pi_h^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl})\to V_h$ satisfy $\Pi_h^1\nabla=\nabla\Pi_h^0$. For $v_h\in V_h\cap B_h^\perp$, put $w_h=(I-P_B)v_h$. Then $w_h\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})\cap B^\perp$, $\operatorname{curl}w_h=\operatorname{curl}v_h$, and
$$\|v_h-w_h\|_2\le\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2.$$
If moreover $\sup_h\|\Pi_h^1\|_{H\to H}\le M$ and $\Pi_h^1f\to f$ in $H$ for each fixed $f\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$, every $H$-convergent sequence of lifts $w_h$ has $\|v_h-w_h\|_2\to0$. Here the $H$ operator norm means that the graph-space operators possess bounded extensions to $H$.

2.1 Write $v_h-w_h=\nabla p_h$ with $p_h\in H_0^1$, and put $e_h=v_h-\Pi_h^1w_h$. Identity on $V_h$ and commutation give $e_h=\Pi_h^1(v_h-w_h)=\nabla\Pi_h^0p_h\in B_h$. Both $v_h$ and $w_h$ are orthogonal to $B_h$, hence $(v_h-w_h,e_h)=0$. Since $v_h-w_h=e_h+(\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h)$, Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\|v_h-w_h\|_2^2=(v_h-w_h,\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h)\le\|v_h-w_h\|_2\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2$. Division if the left factor is nonzero proves the inequality; the zero case is immediate. This is the missing discrete-gradient estimate. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $w_h\to w$ in $H$. The $L^2$ extensions of the projections converge strongly to identity on all $H$: first approximate an arbitrary $f\in H$ by a smooth compactly supported vector field $g$, then use $\|(I-\Pi_h^1)f\|_2\le(1+M)\|f-g\|_2+\|(I-\Pi_h^1)g\|_2$. Consequently $\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2\le(1+M)\|w_h-w\|_2+\|\Pi_h^1w-w\|_2\to0$. Step 2.1 gives the last assertion. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty, bounded, and open. Write $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, $B=\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)$, and let $P_B$ denote the $H$-orthogonal projection onto $B$. Let $S_h\subset H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $V_h\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ be finite-dimensional subspaces with $B_h=\nabla S_h\subset V_h$. Suppose linear projections $\Pi_h^0:H_0^1\to S_h$ and $\Pi_h^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl})\to V_h$ satisfy $\Pi_h^1\nabla=\nabla\Pi_h^0$. For $v_h\in V_h\cap B_h^\perp$, put $w_h=(I-P_B)v_h$. Then $w_h\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})\cap B^\perp$, $\operatorname{curl}w_h=\operatorname{curl}v_h$, and
$$\|v_h-w_h\|_2\le\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2.$$
If moreover $\sup_h\|\Pi_h^1\|_{H\to H}\le M$ and $\Pi_h^1f\to f$ in $H$ for each fixed $f\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$, every $H$-convergent sequence of lifts $w_h$ has $\|v_h-w_h\|_2\to0$. Here the $H$ operator norm means that the graph-space operators possess bounded extensions to $H$.

1.1 If $
abla p_n$ is Cauchy in $H$, [F1] makes $p_n$ Cauchy in $H_0^1$, so its limit $p\in H_0^1$ has $
abla p_n	o
abla p$. Thus $B$ is closed. Apply [F2] to $B$. For its nearest point $P_Bv$, testing the variational inequality with $P_Bv\pm b$, $b\in B$, gives $v-P_Bv\perp B$. Uniqueness of this decomposition proves linearity, and its Pythagorean identity proves that $P_B$ and $I-P_B$ are contractions. Finally, if $p\in H_0^1$, smooth compactly supported approximation shows $
abla p\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ with curl zero: convergence of the gradients is convergence in the curl graph norm. Therefore $w_h=v_h-P_Bv_h$ has the stated membership and curl. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]

2.1 Write $v_h-w_h=\nabla p_h$ with $p_h\in H_0^1$, and put $e_h=v_h-\Pi_h^1w_h$. Identity on $V_h$ and commutation give $e_h=\Pi_h^1(v_h-w_h)=\nabla\Pi_h^0p_h\in B_h$. Both $v_h$ and $w_h$ are orthogonal to $B_h$, hence $(v_h-w_h,e_h)=0$. Since $v_h-w_h=e_h+(\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h)$, Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\|v_h-w_h\|_2^2=(v_h-w_h,\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h)\le\|v_h-w_h\|_2\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2$. Division if the left factor is nonzero proves the inequality; the zero case is immediate. This is the missing discrete-gradient estimate. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the full model of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], let
$h_{k,j}=1/N_{k,j}\to0$, $N_{k,j}\ge3$, and $\tau_k=T/M_k\to0$.
Assume the explicit scheme
[[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]] satisfies its
diffusion-dominance and CFL inequalities at every row, and initialize it by
$U_{k,i}^0=u_0(x_{k,i})$. Its multilinear-in-space, constant-on-time-interval
extensions converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$ to the
unique bounded continuous viscosity solution of the model Cauchy problem.
Such admissible mesh sequences exist for every model in this coefficient
class, so the conclusion also proves existence of that viscosity solution.
Comparison and uniqueness apply among all bounded continuous viscosity
solutions with the prescribed initial trace. There is no additional
comparison hypothesis and no claimed solution-error rate.

## Statement

[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], let
$h_{k,j}=1/N_{k,j}\to0$, $N_{k,j}\ge3$, and $\tau_k=T/M_k\to0$.
Assume the explicit scheme
[[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]] satisfies its
diffusion-dominance and CFL inequalities at every row, and initialize it by
$U_{k,i}^0=u_0(x_{k,i})$. Its multilinear-in-space, constant-on-time-interval
extensions converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$ to the
unique bounded continuous viscosity solution of the model Cauchy problem.
Such admissible mesh sequences exist for every model in this coefficient
class, so the conclusion also proves existence of that viscosity solution.
Comparison and uniqueness apply among all bounded continuous viscosity
solutions with the prescribed initial trace. There is no additional
comparison hypothesis and no claimed solution-error rate.

1.1 Apply [F1] to the given mesh family. Comparison [F2] applies, because [F1] supplies exactly its bounded USC/LSC functions, interior viscosity inequalities and ordered relaxed initial traces. It gives $\overline U\le\underline U$, hence equality by the reverse inequality in [F1]. The conditional implication [F3] now has its premise proved locally, and gives the claimed bounded continuous viscosity solution and convergence on each compact cylinder $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T']$, $T'<T$. Comparing any two bounded continuous solutions in both orders using [F2] proves uniqueness. Full AC is inherited from [F2], and also supplies the Countable Choice used by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 To ensure the existence conclusion is nonvacuous, choose uniform grids $N_{k,j}=N_0+k$ for every $j$, where $$N_0=\max\{3,\lceil B^*/\alpha_*\rceil\}$$ is an integer by [F5]. Put $N=N_0+k$ and $$M_k=\max\{1,\lceil T d(2A^*N^2+B^*N)\rceil\}+k,\qquad\tau_k=T/M_k.$$ Then $|b_j^a|h_j\le B^*/N\le\alpha_*\le\alpha_j^a$, while $$\tau_k\sum_j(2\alpha_j^a/h_j^2+|b_j^a|/h_j)\le (T/M_k)d(2A^*N^2+B^*N)\le1.$$ Thus every row is admissible, $h_{k,j}\to0$, and $\tau_k\le T/k\to0$. The finite recurrence in [F4] produces the numerical arrays on this explicit mesh family. Step 1.1 gives their limit and therefore existence for every stated datum and coefficient family. [F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For all equal states $u$ in the local solver neighborhood,
$G(u,u)=f(u)$. For any finite periodic array of length $n\ge1$ whose adjacent pairs lie in the
local flux domain, define the update (indices modulo $n$)
$$U_j^{new}=U_j-\nu\bigl(G(U_j,U_{j+1})-G(U_{j-1},U_j)\bigr).$$
For any scalar $\nu$, this update using one two-state flux at each interface
preserves the sum of cell states.
